why_wrong: However strong it is, one reused password means a single site's leak exposes all forty accounts.
A plain text file on the desktop can be read by anyone sitting at the machine and by any malware running as his account.
The pattern is obvious once one password leaks, so an attacker can work out the others immediately.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of the authentication factor "something you have"?
options: A one-time code sent to your registered phone
A security question about your first school
Your fingerprint scanned at login
A six-digit PIN you have memorised
questions.explain: The three factor categories are something you know, something you have and something you are. A phone receiving an OTP, an authenticator app, a smart card or a hardware key are all physical items in your possession, so they fall under something you have. Recognising which category each item belongs to is the key to spotting genuine multi-factor authentication.
why_wrong: A security answer is information stored in your memory, so it is something you know.
A fingerprint is a biometric, which is something you are.
A memorised PIN is a secret in your head, so it is something you know.

questions.q: A website asks Meera for her password and then, on the next screen, for a four-digit PIN she chose at signup. She tells her friend the site uses two-factor authentication. Is she right?
options: Yes, because access needs two separate screens
No, because both the password and the PIN are things she knows
No, because multi-factor authentication must use all three categories
Yes, because a PIN counts as something she has
questions.explain: Multi-factor authentication requires evidence from two or more different categories, not simply two steps. A password and a PIN are both secrets stored in her memory, so anyone who learns both, through phishing or a leak, still gets straight in. Pairing the password with a phone code or a fingerprint would make it genuinely multi-factor.
why_wrong: Two prompts on two screens still means two secrets of the same type; the number of screens is not what counts.
Two different categories are enough; using all three is stronger but is not the definition.
A PIN is memorised information, so it is something she knows, not something she has.

questions.q: Withdrawing cash from an ATM using your card and then typing your PIN is an example of:
options: Multi-factor authentication combining something you have with something you know
Single-factor authentication, because both are used at the same machine
Multi-factor authentication combining something you are with something you know
Authorisation rather than authentication
questions.explain: The card is a physical object in your possession and the PIN is a secret in your memory, so the ATM is combining two different categories. That is exactly why a stolen card alone, or an overseen PIN alone, is not enough to take your money. It is the textbook everyday example of two-factor authentication.
why_wrong: Being used at one machine does not merge the two into one factor; the card and the PIN come from different categories.
Nothing biometric is checked at an ordinary ATM; the card is something you have, not something you are.
Authentication is proving who you are, which is precisely what the card and PIN do before any transaction is allowed.

questions.q: Neha's password is captured by a convincing phishing page. The attacker tries to log in but is stopped because the service also asks for a code from Neha's authenticator app. What does this illustrate?
options: That a stolen password alone is no longer enough, because the attacker would also need her second factor
That multi-factor authentication encrypts the password so a phishing page cannot read it
That once multi-factor authentication is on, the password no longer needs to be strong
That multi-factor authentication stopped the phishing email from reaching her
questions.explain: The value of multi-factor authentication is precisely this case: the password is compromised, and the account survives because the attacker cannot produce the second factor. Neha should still change the stolen password immediately, since the second factor is a safety net and not a replacement for password hygiene. An authenticator app also resists SIM swapping better than an SMS code would.
why_wrong: The phishing page did capture the typed password; multi-factor authentication does nothing to encrypt what a user types into a fake site.
Multi-factor authentication adds a layer but does not excuse a weak or reused password, which remains the first line of defence.
Multi-factor authentication controls logins; filtering malicious mail is the job of spam filters and the user's own caution.

questions.q: Why is an authenticator app or a hardware security key usually considered a stronger second factor than an SMS one-time password?
options: SMS codes can be intercepted, and the number can be taken over by SIM swapping
SMS codes count as something you know rather than something you have
An authenticator app removes the need for any password at all
SMS one-time passwords never expire, so they can be reused
questions.explain: An SMS code depends on the phone network and on your mobile operator, and attackers have persuaded operators to move a victim's number to a new SIM in order to receive the codes. An authenticator app or hardware key generates the code on a device you physically hold, with no network path to hijack. SMS is still far better than having no second factor at all.
why_wrong: An SMS code arrives on a device you possess, so it is still something you have; the weakness lies in how it is delivered.
The second factor sits alongside the password; it does not replace it.
One-time passwords are short-lived by design, whichever channel delivers them.

questions.q: A firewall is best described as:
options: A system that monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and allows or blocks it according to configured rules
A program that scans stored files and removes infected ones
A service that encrypts your traffic so it cannot be read in transit
A tool that keeps a second copy of your data in case of loss
questions.explain: A firewall sits between a trusted machine or network and an untrusted one such as the Internet, and checks traffic against a rulebook with a default policy, usually deny unless explicitly allowed. It can be hardware, software, or both. Think of it as a gatekeeper deciding what may pass, not as something that inspects or repairs the machine itself.
why_wrong: That describes antivirus software, which works on files on the machine rather than on traffic crossing the boundary.
Encrypting traffic is the job of a VPN or of HTTPS; a firewall filters traffic but does not conceal it.
That describes a backup system, which is unrelated to filtering network traffic.

questions.q: A simple packet-filtering firewall decides whether to allow a packet mainly by looking at:
options: The source and destination addresses and the port numbers
The name of the user who is currently logged in to the computer
Whether the file being transferred matches a known virus signature
Whether the person at the keyboard has typed the correct password
questions.explain: Packet filtering is the simplest kind of firewall rule: it compares each packet's source and destination address and port against the rulebook and allows or denies it, with deny unless allowed as the usual default. More advanced firewalls go further by tracking the state of a connection or inspecting the application content inside the traffic. In every case the decision is about traffic crossing the boundary, not about the contents of the disk.
why_wrong: Packet filter rules are written in terms of addresses and ports, not in terms of whichever person happens to be signed in at that moment.
Comparing files against virus signatures is antivirus work; a packet filter does not scan for malware signatures.
Checking a password is authentication done by the service being reached, not a filtering decision made on each packet.

questions.q: Karan's laptop is hit by ransomware after he downloads a cracked copy of a paid program. He protests that his firewall was switched on the whole time. What is the correct explanation?
options: A firewall filters network traffic against rules; it cannot remove or stop malware he chose to download and run on the machine
A hardware firewall would have deleted the ransomware, but a software firewall cannot
A firewall only inspects outgoing traffic, so it never sees anything arriving
The firewall failed only because it was not set to deny by default; a correct rulebook removes malware
questions.explain: Firewalls decide what traffic may cross a boundary; they do not examine or clean files running on the machine. Karan personally authorised the download and then executed it, so the traffic looked like ordinary permitted web use. Protection here would have come from not running untrusted software, plus antivirus and up-to-date backups.
why_wrong: Hardware firewalls protect a whole network at its edge, but they also filter traffic rather than remove malware from a computer.
Firewalls inspect both incoming and outgoing traffic; direction is not the issue here.
No firewall rulebook, however strict, removes malware from disk; that is the job of antivirus software.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a hardware firewall from a software firewall?
options: A hardware firewall is a separate device, often built into the router, protecting a whole network; a software firewall runs on one computer and protects that machine
A hardware firewall protects a single computer; a software firewall protects the entire network from the router
A software firewall can only block outgoing traffic, while a hardware firewall only blocks incoming traffic
A hardware firewall only records traffic for later review, while a software firewall actually blocks it
questions.explain: The difference is where the firewall sits and how much it covers. A hardware firewall guards the boundary of a whole network, so every device behind it benefits; a software firewall such as Windows Defender Firewall protects only the computer it runs on, including when that laptop is on someone else's network. Using both together is common and sensible.
why_wrong: This reverses the two: the separate device at the network edge is the hardware firewall.
Both kinds can filter traffic in either direction; the rules decide, not the form factor.
Both kinds enforce allow and deny decisions; logging is an extra feature, not the distinction.

questions.q: The principle of least privilege states that:
options: Every user and program should have only the minimum access needed to do its job, and no more
Everyday work should be done in the administrator account so that prompts do not interrupt it
Everyone in a lab should share one account so that settings stay consistent
All users should be given administrator rights, provided their passwords are strong
questions.explain: Least privilege limits the damage any single account or program can do if it is misused or compromised. It is why operating systems separate administrator, standard and guest accounts in the first place, and why you elevate only for the specific task that needs it. Less standing power means a smaller blast radius when something goes wrong.
why_wrong: Working as administrator is the opposite of least privilege, since anything that runs then inherits full control of the system.
A shared account destroys accountability, because no action can be traced to the person who performed it.
Strong passwords do not reduce what malware can do once it is running with administrator rights.

questions.q: Yash does all his coursework and browsing while logged in as Administrator. A friend advises him to use a standard account for daily work instead. Why is that safer?
options: Malware that runs in a standard account inherits only that account's limited rights and cannot silently change system-wide settings or other users' files
A standard account automatically scans every download for viruses before it opens
Malware simply cannot execute at all inside a standard account
A standard account encrypts everything he downloads from the Internet
questions.explain: A program runs with the privileges of the account that starts it, so working as a standard user puts a ceiling on what any malicious program can reach. It might damage his own files, but it cannot quietly install itself system-wide or touch other users' data without an administrator password. When he genuinely needs to install something, he elevates deliberately for that one task.
why_wrong: Account type does not provide malware scanning; that is antivirus software's job.
Malware can still run as a standard user; what changes is how much it is permitted to affect.
Standard accounts do not encrypt downloads; encryption is a separate feature entirely.

questions.q: Which statement about a Guest account is correct?
options: It is a temporary, heavily restricted account that cannot install software or reach other users' files
It has the same rights as a standard user, just with a different password
It can install software as long as the software is installed only for the guest
It is the Windows name for the Linux root account
questions.explain: A guest account exists so a visitor can use a machine briefly without gaining any lasting access. It is deliberately the most restricted of the account types: no installing, no system changes, and no reading of other people's files. Administrator, standard and guest form a ladder of decreasing privilege.
why_wrong: A guest is more restricted than a standard user, who at least keeps their own files and settings between sessions.
Installing software is exactly what a guest account is prevented from doing.
Root on Linux is the fully privileged account, which is the opposite of a guest.

questions.q: On a shared Linux lab machine, Priya's attempt to install a compiler fails with a permission denied message. She normally works in her own ordinary account. What is the best thing to do?
options: Run just that one installation command with sudo and then carry on working as her normal user
Log in as root and stay as root for the rest of the session so nothing is blocked again
Change the permissions on the system directories so no command needs privileges
Give her own account permanent administrator rights so the prompts never appear again
questions.explain: Elevating briefly and deliberately for the single command that needs it is exactly what sudo on Linux, and Run as administrator with its UAC prompt on Windows, are designed for. The moment the command finishes she is back to limited rights, so anything else she runs cannot touch the system. Staying elevated turns a one-minute need into a session-long risk.
why_wrong: Remaining root means every later command, including a mistyped or malicious one, runs with full system power.
Loosening permissions on system directories removes the protection for every user on the machine and is far worse than the original problem.
Permanent elevation defeats least privilege; the point is to hold the power only while it is actually needed.

questions.q: A shopping site's address bar shows https:// and a closed padlock icon. By itself, what does this prove?
options: The connection between your browser and that site is encrypted
The site is run by an honest business and is safe to buy from
The site has been scanned and found free of malware
The identity of the site's owner has been verified by the government
questions.explain: HTTPS with the padlock means the traffic between you and that server is encrypted, so someone eavesdropping on the network cannot read it. It says nothing about the honesty of whoever is on the other end, because criminals can obtain certificates just as easily as anyone else. That is why you still have to read the domain name carefully for look-alike spellings before trusting a page.
why_wrong: Honesty is not certified by a padlock at all, and phishing sites routinely use HTTPS so that they look trustworthy.
No malware scan is involved in getting a certificate; the padlock only concerns how the data travels.
An ordinary certificate confirms control of the domain name, not a government check on who the owner is.

questions.q: Riya is at a cafe using its free open Wi-Fi and wants to pay her hostel fee through her bank's website. What is the safest thing for her to do?
options: Go ahead on the cafe Wi-Fi, since the bank site uses HTTPS and that makes any network safe
Switch to her own mobile data, or use a VPN if she must stay on the cafe Wi-Fi
Ask the staff for the Wi-Fi password, because a password-protected network is private
Open the bank site in a private or incognito window while on the cafe Wi-Fi
questions.explain: Public or free Wi-Fi should be treated as untrusted, so banking and password entry are best done off it. Her own mobile data avoids the untrusted network entirely, and a VPN encrypts all her traffic through a secure tunnel if she has to stay connected. Encryption of the path is exactly what the risk calls for here.
why_wrong: HTTPS protects the contents of the connection, but it does not remove the other risks of an untrusted network, such as a fake hotspot steering you to a look-alike site.
A Wi-Fi password printed on the menu is known to every customer, so the network is shared, not private.
A private window only stops history and cookies being saved on that device; it does not encrypt your traffic or hide it from the network.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a PASSIVE digital footprint?
options: Uploading a photo of a college fest to your social media account
Cookies recording which websites you visited and for how long
Writing a review of a restaurant on a maps app
Filling in an online scholarship application form
questions.explain: A passive footprint is data collected about you without any deliberate act of sharing, such as your IP address, cookies, browsing history, location and device details. An active footprint is what you knowingly put online yourself. The test is simple: did you choose to publish it, or was it gathered while you were just using the service?
why_wrong: Uploading a photo is a deliberate act of sharing, which makes it an active footprint.
Writing and publishing a review is something you consciously post, so it is active.
Typing your details into a form is deliberate sharing, so this is an active footprint too.

questions.q: In the college computer lab, Neha finds that the previous user, her friend Priya, walked away leaving her email account signed in, with several unread messages visible. What should Neha do?
options: Read the unread messages to see whether anything is urgent, then tell Priya about them
Sign the account out without reading anything, and tell Priya she left it open
Change the account password so nobody else can get in, and pass the new one to Priya
Screenshot the inbox and send it to Priya on WhatsApp as proof that she left it open
questions.explain: Two rules meet here. Accounts on shared or public computers must always be logged out, so closing the session is the right protective step. And respecting privacy means not reading someone else's messages even when nothing technically stops you and even when you mean well.
why_wrong: Reading her messages is a privacy violation; being able to see them does not make it acceptable.
Changing someone else's password without permission is interference with an account that is not yours, and it can lock her out.
A screenshot copies her private inbox onto your phone and into a chat, which spreads the exposure instead of ending it.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a safe internet practice?
options: Installing operating system and browser updates soon after they are released
Granting an app every permission it asks for so that it works properly
Installing software only from the official website or an official app store
Locking your phone and laptop with a PIN, password or biometric
questions.explain: Permissions should be reviewed, not handed over automatically: an app only needs access that matches what it does, so a torch app asking for your contacts and location is a warning sign. Granting everything gives an app far more of your data than its job requires. The other three are standard protective habits.
why_wrong: Updates mostly exist to close security holes that attackers are already exploiting, so installing them quickly is good practice.
Official sources are the safest supply route, since cracked or modified software is a common way of delivering trojans.
A screen lock is the basic protection for a device that could be lost, stolen or simply left unattended.

questions.q: Arjun's laptop is hit by ransomware: his project files are encrypted and a note demands payment to unlock them. He has no copies anywhere else. Which habit would have let him recover without paying?
options: Keeping regular backups of important files, with at least one copy kept offline
Using a longer and stronger password on his laptop account
Browsing only in private or incognito mode
Storing the files in a hidden folder with an unusual name
questions.explain: Ransomware works by making your only copy unreadable, so the reliable answer is having another copy it cannot reach. An offline backup matters because a drive or sync folder that stays connected can be encrypted along with everything else. Paying is never a guarantee that the files come back.
why_wrong: A strong password protects the account from being guessed, but it does nothing once malware is already running on the machine.
Private browsing only avoids saving history and cookies locally; it neither blocks malware nor restores files.
Hiding or renaming a folder does not stop encryption software, which simply works through the files it finds.

questions.q: Which statement about your digital footprint is correct?
options: Deleting a post guarantees the content is gone from the internet
Content can survive deletion in caches, screenshots and archives, and may resurface years later
Your footprint is stored only on your own device, so wiping the device erases it
Only well-known public figures have a digital footprint worth worrying about
questions.explain: A digital footprint is persistent, searchable and easy to copy, so deleting the original does not recall the copies other people and systems already hold. This matters because colleges, scholarship committees and employers routinely search for applicants. The practical takeaway is to think before you post, because that is the one point where you have full control.
why_wrong: Once content has been cached, archived or screenshotted by someone else, deleting your copy does not remove theirs.
The trail sits on other companies' servers, in other users' copies and in archives, so wiping your own device removes none of it.
Anyone who uses the internet leaves a trail, and ordinary students are searched by admissions and recruiters too.

questions.q: Kabir copies three paragraphs from a blog into his assignment report, changes a few words here and there, and submits it with no mention of where the text came from. How should this be judged?
options: Acceptable, because the blog is freely available to read on the internet
Plagiarism, because material taken from a source must be credited whether or not it is free to read
Acceptable, because he rewrote some of the words rather than copying them exactly
Acceptable, because he is not selling the report or making money from it
questions.explain: Respecting intellectual property is a core part of cyber ethics, and plagiarism is presenting someone else's work as your own. Free access is about reading, not about ownership, so the author still deserves credit. Quoting or paraphrasing is fine as long as you cite the source.
why_wrong: Free to read is not the same as free to reuse without credit; the author still holds rights over the work.
Swapping a few words leaves the ideas and structure as someone else's, which is still plagiarism.
Plagiarism is about false credit, not profit, so a non-commercial report is judged the same way.

questions.q: A forwarded message reaches Sana's class group claiming that a well-known bank is collapsing and that everyone should withdraw their money today. It names no source. What is the ethical response?
options: Forward it to her family groups at once, since it is better to be safe than sorry
Check it against the bank's official announcements or a reliable news source, and not forward it unless it is verified
Forward it only to a few close friends, since a small group cannot cause any harm
Forward it with a note saying she is not sure it is true, leaving readers to decide
questions.explain: Not spreading misinformation is part of cyber ethics: verify before forwarding, and do not amplify rumours. An unverified financial rumour can cause real panic and real losses, so the cost of forwarding it is not zero. If you cannot confirm it, the right action is to stop it with you.
why_wrong: Forwarding first and checking later is exactly how a rumour spreads, and it can trigger the panic the message describes.
Small groups forward onward too, so limited sharing still starts a chain and still lends the rumour your credibility.
A disclaimer does not undo the spread; you have still passed on unverified content and taken responsibility for it.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of cyberbullying?
options: Repeatedly posting mocking comments about a classmate's photo in a class group
Forwarding a health claim to friends without checking whether it is true
Downloading a paid film from a pirate site instead of paying for it
Typing a whole message in capital letters in a group chat
questions.explain: Cyberbullying is using online channels to harass, mock, threaten or humiliate a person, especially repeatedly. The guiding idea in cyber ethics is that behaviour which would be wrong face to face is equally wrong online, because there is a real person on the other side. The other three options are also failures of cyber ethics, but each is a different one.
why_wrong: This is spreading misinformation: the failure is not verifying before forwarding, rather than targeting a person.
This is piracy, a violation of copyright and intellectual property rather than harassment of someone.
Writing in all capitals reads as shouting, which is poor netiquette; it is rude, not bullying.

questions.q: Which Git command makes a complete local copy of a repository that already exists on GitHub?
options: git init
git status
git clone
git commit
questions.explain: git clone takes the address of an existing repository and downloads the whole project into a new folder on your computer, including its full history. It is the normal way to start working on a project that someone has already put online. What you get is a complete repository, not just the latest files.
why_wrong: git init creates a brand-new empty repository in a folder on your own machine; it downloads nothing.
git status only reports which files in your working folder have been changed or staged.
git commit records staged changes in the history of a repository you already have.

questions.q: In a botnet, what is a single infected computer that obeys the attacker's instructions usually called?
options: a rootkit
a firewall
a phishing page
a bot, also called a zombie
questions.explain: A botnet is built from many ordinary machines that have been infected and quietly taken over. Each such machine is called a bot, or a zombie, because it does the attacker's bidding while its owner notices nothing. The owner usually keeps using the computer normally the whole time.
why_wrong: A rootkit is malware that hides itself and the attacker's activity deep inside the operating system.
A firewall is a protective control that filters network traffic; it is not an infected machine.
A phishing page is a fake web page built to capture the details a user types into it.

questions.q: In Git, what is a repository?
options: the storage for a project's files together with the complete history of changes made to them
a single file listing the names of everyone working on the project
an online forum where programmers discuss a project
a compressed backup copy of a folder taken once a week
questions.explain: A repository is the project plus its memory. Alongside the current files it keeps every recorded change, with the author and time of each one, so any earlier state can be inspected or restored. This is what separates a repository from an ordinary folder of files.
why_wrong: A list of contributors is just an ordinary text file; a repository holds the project itself along with its history.
Discussion happens in places such as GitHub issues, not in the repository storage itself.
A weekly compressed backup keeps a single snapshot, while a repository keeps every recorded change and who made it.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of antivirus software?
options: to speed up the computer by deleting temporary files
to detect, block and remove malicious software on a computer
to encrypt the files on a disk so that others cannot read them
to copy documents to an external drive automatically
questions.explain: Antivirus software exists to find malicious programs and stop them doing harm. It checks files and running programs against what it knows about malware, blocks anything dangerous, and removes or isolates what it finds. Tidying, encrypting and backing up are separate jobs done by other tools.
why_wrong: Clearing temporary files is the work of disk cleanup tools and does nothing about malware.
Encrypting a disk so others cannot read it is the job of disk-encryption software.
Automatic copying of documents to another drive is what backup software does.

questions.q: Which command displays the configuration settings Git is currently using, such as the stored user name and email?
options: git log
git diff
git init
git config --list
questions.explain: git config --list prints out the settings Git has in effect, so you can check values such as user.name and user.email without guessing. It is the usual way to confirm that configuration was saved where you expected. Reading settings this way is separate from setting them, which uses the same git config command with a value.
why_wrong: git log prints the history of commits, not the settings Git is using.
git diff shows the line-by-line changes in your files.
git init turns a folder into a new repository.

questions.q: When antivirus software quarantines a file, what has it done with that file?
options: moved it to an isolated area where it cannot run or affect other files
sent it to the police for investigation
renamed it and left it working normally
encrypted every other file on the disk as a precaution
questions.explain: Quarantine is a holding area. The suspicious file is moved there and stripped of the ability to run, so it can do no damage, but it is not destroyed straight away. That matters because if the detection turns out to be a mistake, the file can still be restored.
why_wrong: Antivirus software isolates a suspicious file locally; it reports nothing to any authority.
A quarantined file is deliberately prevented from running, so leaving it working would defeat the purpose.
Encrypting everything on a disk is what ransomware does, not what protective software does.

questions.q: In Git, what is a branch?
options: a folder inside the project that stores images and other media
a separate line of development that lets work continue without disturbing the main version
a copy of the project uploaded to GitHub for other people to download
a short message attached to a commit describing what was changed
questions.explain: A branch is an independent line of commits inside the same repository. Work done on one branch does not change the others, so a new feature or experiment can be developed while the main version stays as it is. The branches can later be brought back together by merging.
why_wrong: Folders for images and other media are ordinary project folders and have nothing to do with branching.
A copy uploaded so that others can take it is a remote repository or a clone, not a branch.
A short description attached to a commit is the commit message.

questions.q: Why should antivirus software be updated regularly?
options: so that it makes the computer run faster after every update
so that it can recover files the user deleted by mistake
so that it can recognise newly discovered malware and not only older known threats
so that it can copy the user's documents to online storage
questions.explain: New malware appears constantly, so an antivirus program can only recognise what it has been taught about. Updates keep its knowledge of threats current, and they also fix faults in the program itself. An antivirus left un-updated for months slowly becomes blind to the newest attacks.
why_wrong: Antivirus updates are about recognising threats, not about tuning performance.
Recovering deleted files is the job of backup or recovery tools.
Copying documents to online storage is a backup service and is unrelated to antivirus updates.

questions.q: Which command creates a new branch and switches to it in a single step?
options: git checkout -b feature
git merge feature
git clone feature
git add feature
questions.explain: git checkout -b feature makes a branch called feature and immediately moves you onto it, so the next commits you make belong to that branch. Without the -b option, checkout only switches to a branch that already exists. It is the usual quick way to begin a piece of separate work.
why_wrong: git merge brings the changes of another branch into the branch you are on; it creates no new branch.
git clone copies an entire repository from another location and is not used to make branches.
git add stages changed files so that they go into the next commit.

questions.q: Which of the following is a type of malware?
options: Firewall
Password manager
Version control system
Rootkit
questions.explain: Malware is software written to harm a system or its user, and a rootkit is one of the named types: it buries itself in the operating system to keep hidden control for an attacker. The other three are ordinary useful tools, two of them protective. Recognising which names belong to attacks and which to defences is the first step in this topic.
why_wrong: A firewall is a protective control that filters the traffic entering or leaving a computer or network.
A password manager is a helpful tool that stores and fills in strong passwords.
A version control system records the history of changes made to a project's files.

questions.q: Run on its own with no extra arguments, what does the command git branch do?
options: deletes every branch except the main one
sends the current branch to GitHub
lists the branches in the repository and marks the one you are currently on
joins two branches together
questions.explain: Plain git branch is a reporting command: it prints the branches that exist in the repository and puts a marker next to the branch you are working on. Creating and deleting branches need extra arguments or options. Running it is a safe way to get your bearings before starting work.
why_wrong: Git removes a branch only when you explicitly ask it to with the delete option.
Sending a branch to GitHub is done with git push.
Joining two branches together is the job of git merge.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common sign that a computer may be infected with malware?
options: programs crash often, the machine becomes unusually slow and unfamiliar pop-ups appear
the keyboard layout changes after the user selects a different language
a document takes longer to print when the printer has run out of paper
the battery drains faster while a demanding game is running
questions.explain: Malware runs without permission and consumes resources, interferes with programs and often displays things the user never asked for, so frequent crashes, sudden slowness and strange pop-ups together are a classic warning. No single symptom proves an infection, but that combination deserves a full scan. The other behaviours listed all have plain, innocent explanations.
why_wrong: Changing the layout is exactly the expected result of the user choosing another language.
A printer that has run out of paper explains the delay perfectly well on its own.
Heavier programs use more power, so faster battery drain during a game is normal behaviour.

questions.q: Which command lists the remote repositories your local repository is connected to, together with their URLs?
options: git status
git remote -v
git log --oneline
git branch
questions.explain: git remote -v prints the short names of the remotes, such as origin, next to the addresses they point to. It is how you confirm that your repository is pointing at the GitHub project you think it is. The -v stands for verbose, which is what adds the URLs to the list.
why_wrong: git status reports the state of your working folder and staging area.
git log --oneline prints a compact list of past commits.
git branch lists the branches inside your repository.

questions.q: In the study of malware, what is meant by the payload?
options: the size of the malware file in megabytes
the e-mail account used to send the malware
the harmful action the malware actually carries out on the victim's system
the password the attacker uses to log in to the victim's account
questions.explain: Malware has two separate parts to think about: how it gets in and spreads, and what it does once it is there. The payload is the second part, the damage itself, such as encrypting files, stealing data or opening a back door. Two pieces of malware can spread in the same way and still carry completely different payloads.
why_wrong: The size of the file says nothing about what the malware does once it runs.
The account used to send it is a delivery detail, not the harmful action itself.
The attacker's own login details are not part of what the malware carries.

questions.q: On GitHub, what is the usual purpose of a project's README file?
options: to list the files Git should ignore
to record the author name and email used for commits
to store the passwords needed to run the project
to introduce the project and explain what it does and how to use it
questions.explain: GitHub displays the README straight under the file list on a project's page, so it is the first thing a visitor reads. It is where the project explains its purpose, how to install or run it, and how someone can contribute. A clear README is often what decides whether a stranger bothers with a project at all.
why_wrong: The list of files Git should not track belongs in .gitignore.
The author name and email come from Git's configuration, not from a file in the project.
Passwords and other secrets must never be placed in a repository at all.

questions.q: Why do security experts advise victims of ransomware not to pay the ransom?
options: paying is impossible because ransomware provides no way to pay
paying gives no guarantee that the files will be restored, and the money funds further attacks
paying automatically deletes the encrypted files
paying repairs the files but permanently disables the antivirus software
questions.explain: The person demanding the money is a criminal, so there is nothing to make them keep their side of the bargain, and many victims who pay never receive a working key. Payment also marks the victim as willing to pay and finances the next round of attacks. This is why keeping good offline backups matters far more than deciding what to do after the demand appears.
why_wrong: Attackers always supply a payment method; the demand would be pointless otherwise.
Payment does not delete anything; the files stay encrypted until a key is applied.
There is no mechanism by which a payment repairs files or switches off protective software.

questions.q: When a folder has been turned into a Git repository, which hidden directory inside it holds the project's history and settings?
options: .git
.gitignore
.github
.config
questions.explain: All of Git's own data lives in a hidden directory named .git at the top of the project. It contains the recorded commits, the branches and the repository's local configuration, which is why deleting that directory turns the folder back into ordinary files. You never edit it by hand; Git manages it through its commands.
why_wrong: .gitignore is a single text file listing what Git should not track; it stores no history.
.github is a folder some projects add for GitHub-specific settings, not the repository's history.
.config is an ordinary folder name used by various programs and has no special meaning to Git.

questions.q: Ransomware demands are usually made in which form of payment?
options: a cheque posted to the attacker's bank
cash handed over in person
a card payment to a registered company
cryptocurrency, because it is hard to trace back to the attacker
questions.explain: Attackers need to collect money without revealing who they are, and cryptocurrency transfers can be made to an anonymous address from anywhere in the world. Ordinary payment methods are tied to identifiable accounts or businesses that investigators can follow. The demand is also usually given a short deadline to pressure the victim into acting before thinking.
why_wrong: A cheque carries account details that can be traced, so attackers avoid it.
Meeting the victim in person would expose the attacker at once.
A registered company account could be identified and frozen, which is exactly what an attacker avoids.

questions.q: In the command git commit -m "Add login page", what does the -m option do?
options: it merges the current branch into the main branch
it moves the committed files into a new folder
it supplies the commit message inside the same command
it marks the commit so that it can never be changed later
questions.explain: Every commit needs a message describing the change, and -m lets you type that message right there in quotes instead of having Git open an editor for it. The message becomes part of the recorded history and is what your teammates read in the log later. Without -m, Git simply asks for the message another way.
why_wrong: Merging one branch into another is done with git merge, not with an option of git commit.
Committing never moves your files; it records their contents in the history.
Nothing in git commit -m locks a commit; the option only carries the message.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common way for malware to get onto a computer?
options: running a program downloaded from an untrusted website
setting a long, unique password for each account
turning on multi-factor authentication for an account
installing the latest operating system updates
questions.explain: Most infections begin with the user running something they should not have, and files from untrusted websites are a favourite carrier because the attacker controls exactly what is inside them. Downloading only from official sites and app stores removes a large share of the risk. The other three choices are protective habits, not routes in.
why_wrong: A long, unique password protects an account and cannot bring malware onto a machine.
Multi-factor authentication adds a second check at login, so it is a defence rather than a way in.
Applying updates closes the weaknesses malware relies on, which lowers the risk instead of creating it.

questions.q: In the command git add . , what does the dot stand for?
options: only the file that was edited most recently
all the changed files in the current directory and the directories inside it
the hidden configuration folder of the repository
the most recent commit in the history
questions.explain: In file paths a dot means the current directory, so git add . stages everything that has changed there and in the folders below it. That saves naming each file, but it also means you should check git status first so that nothing unwanted is swept in. Files listed in .gitignore are still left out.
why_wrong: Git has no option that stages only the newest edit; the dot means a whole directory.
Git's own hidden storage is managed by Git itself and is never staged by you.
Commits already in the history are not something git add works on.

questions.q: Which habit reduces the chance of picking up malware from a USB drive?
options: copying all its files to the desktop before opening them
renaming the files on the drive before opening them
scanning the drive with antivirus software before opening anything on it
opening the files with a different program from the usual one
questions.explain: Removable drives pass between many machines, so one infected computer can pass malware to every drive plugged into it. Scanning the drive before opening anything gives the antivirus a chance to spot known malware while nothing has been run yet. Being cautious with drives whose history you do not know is part of the same habit.
why_wrong: Copying the files onto your own machine first brings the danger closer instead of removing it.
A file's name has no effect on what the code inside it does when it runs.
Choosing another program does not change whether the file itself is malicious.

questions.q: Phishing is best described as:
options: Flooding a website with so much traffic that genuine users can no longer reach it
Secretly recording every key a user presses on the keyboard
Sending fake messages that appear to come from a trusted organisation in order to trick the reader into revealing sensitive information
Scrambling a message so that only the intended receiver can read it
questions.explain: Phishing is a deception attack. The attacker imitates a bank, a college or a well-known service so that the reader trusts the message and hands over passwords, OTPs or card details. Nothing is broken into technically; the victim is persuaded to give the information away.
why_wrong: That describes a denial-of-service attack, which attacks a service's availability rather than deceiving a person.
That describes a keylogger, a form of spyware; phishing works by fooling the reader, not by secretly installed recording software.
That describes encryption, which is a protective measure rather than an attack.

questions.q: Phishing that is carried out through SMS text messages is called:
options: Vishing
Smishing
Whaling
Pretexting
questions.explain: The name joins SMS with phishing. The trick is the same as in email phishing, only the delivery channel changes: a text message carries a scare or an offer and a link to a fake site. Each phishing channel has its own name, which is why the terms are worth separating.
why_wrong: Vishing is phishing carried out by voice call, where the attacker speaks to the victim.
Whaling is a phishing attack aimed at a senior figure such as a chief executive or a principal.
Pretexting is inventing a believable scenario and false identity in order to extract information.

questions.q: Watching a person from close by as they type a password or PIN, in order to learn it, is called:
options: Baiting
Tailgating
Dumpster diving
Shoulder surfing
questions.explain: Shoulder surfing needs no software at all, only a clear view of the keyboard, the screen or the ATM keypad. It is a reminder that information can leak through ordinary observation, which is why people shield the keypad while entering a PIN.
why_wrong: Baiting tempts the victim with something attractive, such as a USB drive left where it will be picked up.
Tailgating is following an authorised person through a secured door without using your own credentials.
Dumpster diving is searching discarded papers, printouts and old devices for useful information.

questions.q: In social engineering, offering the victim something in return, such as free technical help, in exchange for information or access is known as:
options: Quid pro quo
Dumpster diving
Smishing
Whaling
questions.explain: Quid pro quo means something for something. The attacker poses as a helper, for example a support engineer offering to fix a problem, and asks for a password or for remote access as the price of that help. The apparent favour is what lowers the victim's guard.
why_wrong: Dumpster diving gathers information from an organisation's rubbish, without any contact with the victim.
Smishing is phishing delivered by SMS text message.
Whaling is a phishing attack aimed specifically at a senior figure in an organisation.

questions.q: Entering a restricted area by walking in closely behind an authorised person, instead of using your own card or key, is called:
options: Pretexting
Vishing
Tailgating
Baiting
questions.explain: Tailgating is a physical social-engineering technique: the attacker never defeats the lock, he relies on a person's politeness in holding the door. It works because refusing to let someone in feels rude, which is exactly the instinct the attacker is counting on.
why_wrong: Pretexting is building a false story and identity to draw information out of someone.
Vishing is phishing carried out over a voice call.
Baiting leaves something tempting, such as a labelled USB drive, for the victim to pick up and use.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common warning sign that an email is a phishing attempt?
options: A newsletter you subscribed to yourself, arriving on its usual day
An urgent warning that your account will be closed within hours unless you click a link and confirm your details
A reply from a classmate inside a conversation that you started
A message from your college that greets you by name and asks for nothing
questions.explain: Manufactured urgency is one of the clearest phishing signals. A threat with a deadline is meant to push the reader into clicking before thinking, and genuine organisations do not demand account details through a link in an unexpected message. Slowing down and checking through the official app or printed helpline number defeats it.
why_wrong: A newsletter you signed up for and expect is ordinary mail and shows none of the pressure tactics of phishing.
A reply inside a thread you began yourself is normal correspondence; phishing typically arrives unannounced.
Being greeted by name and being asked for nothing are the opposite of the usual signs, which are a vague Dear Customer greeting and a demand for information.

questions.q: In social engineering, pretending to be someone else, such as a colleague or an IT support engineer, is called:
options: Dumpster diving
Shoulder surfing
Baiting
Impersonation
questions.explain: Impersonation means assuming a false identity that the victim already trusts, so that requests which would normally be refused seem routine. A claimed role such as help desk, courier or senior staff member carries authority, and that borrowed authority is the whole attack.
why_wrong: Dumpster diving collects information from discarded papers and devices rather than by adopting an identity.
Shoulder surfing is reading a password or PIN by watching the person type it.
Baiting relies on leaving something tempting for the victim to pick up and use.

questions.q: A link inside a phishing email most often leads the victim to:
options: A fake website built to look like the real one, which records whatever is typed into it
The organisation's genuine login page, exactly as it normally appears
A page that automatically repairs the victim's account
The settings screen of the victim's own computer
questions.explain: The fake page is the point of the whole message. It copies the logo, layout and wording of the real site, so anything typed into it, usually a username, password or OTP, is delivered straight to the attacker. This is why the address in the bar matters more than the look of the page.
why_wrong: If the link opened the genuine page there would be nothing for the attacker to capture; phishing links point to look-alike domains instead.
No web page repairs an account by itself; that promise is only part of the bait.
A link in an email opens a page in the browser and cannot open the computer's own settings.

questions.q: Multi-factor authentication means that signing in to an account requires:
options: A password that is at least twelve characters long
Signing in from two different devices at the same time
Two or more pieces of evidence of identity taken from different categories, such as something you know and something you have
Two separate accounts on the same website
questions.explain: The strength of multi-factor authentication comes from combining different kinds of proof. A stolen password is only one kind, so an attacker who has it still cannot get in without the phone, the app code or the fingerprint that supplies the second kind.
why_wrong: A long password is a matter of password strength; however long it is, it is still a single factor.
Using two devices at once is not what the term means; the requirement is two different kinds of proof, not two machines.
Holding a second account provides no extra evidence of who you are.

questions.q: The three usual categories of authentication factors are described as:
options: Something you type, something you click, something you scroll
Something you know, something you have, something you are
Something public, something private, something shared
Something you buy, something you borrow, something you build
questions.explain: Something you know covers passwords and PINs, something you have covers a phone, a card or a security key, and something you are covers fingerprints and face recognition. Genuine multi-factor authentication draws on more than one of these three groups.
why_wrong: These describe ways of using a keyboard and mouse, not categories of identity evidence.
Public, private and shared describe how keys or files are shared, not how a person proves identity.
This is not a recognised grouping; the standard three are know, have and are.

questions.q: Which of these tasks normally needs an administrator account rather than a standard user account?
options: Opening a browser and reading a news website
Saving a document inside your own home folder
Playing a music file already stored on the machine
Installing a program for every user of the computer
questions.explain: Anything that changes the system as a whole, such as installing software for all users, altering system files or changing security settings, is reserved for administrators. Everyday work touches only the user's own files and therefore needs no such rights.
why_wrong: Browsing the web is ordinary activity that any standard account can do.
Your home folder belongs to your own account, so writing inside it needs no elevated rights.
Playing a file you already have access to affects nothing outside your session.

questions.q: On a Linux system, the account that has complete administrative control over the machine is called:
options: root
guest
home
user
questions.explain: root is the superuser account on Linux, able to read, change or delete anything on the system. Because a mistake or a piece of malware running as root affects the whole machine, everyday work is done in an ordinary account instead.
why_wrong: guest is a temporary, heavily restricted account, which is the opposite of complete control.
/home is the directory that holds users' personal folders; it is a location, not an account.
user is a general word for anyone with an account and is not the name of the all-powerful one.

questions.q: On a Linux system, the sudo command lets a permitted ordinary user:
options: Permanently convert their own account into an administrator account
Delete any file without it going to the trash
Run a single command with administrator (superuser) privileges
Log in to another computer across the network
questions.explain: sudo raises privileges for one command only, after which the user is back to normal rights. That narrow window is what makes it safer than logging in as root, because anything that goes wrong is limited to the one command that was elevated.
why_wrong: The account's own type is unchanged; sudo grants elevated rights for a command, not a permanent promotion.
Bypassing the trash is a matter of how a file is deleted and has nothing to do with privilege.
Connecting to another machine over the network is the job of ssh.

questions.q: An attack in which a program tries every possible combination of characters until the correct password is found is called:
options: Shoulder surfing
A brute force attack
Credential stuffing
A phishing attack
questions.explain: A brute force attack simply exhausts the possibilities, so its only enemy is the size of the search space. Every extra character multiplies the number of combinations, which is why length is the single most useful property of a password against this attack.
why_wrong: Shoulder surfing learns a password by watching the person type it, with no guessing involved.
Credential stuffing reuses username and password pairs already leaked from another site rather than generating combinations.
Phishing persuades the user to hand the password over, so nothing has to be guessed.

questions.q: The letters OTP, used for the short code a bank sends to your registered phone, stand for:
options: Online Transaction Protocol
Open Terminal Password
Official Transfer PIN
One-Time Password
questions.explain: A one-time password is valid for a single use and only for a short period, so it cannot be reused later even if someone sees it. It usually serves as the second factor, proving possession of the registered phone in addition to the password you know.
why_wrong: There is no such protocol; OTP names a code, not a way of moving data.
Terminal access is unrelated; the code is not tied to any terminal.
The code is not restricted to transfers and is not a fixed PIN that you choose.

questions.q: Your digital footprint is:
options: The trail of data you leave behind through your activity online
The amount of disk space your files take up on your computer
The number of devices connected to your home router
The physical size of the screen you browse on
questions.explain: Every search, post, purchase and site visit leaves a record somewhere, and together those records form your digital footprint. It matters because colleges, employers and advertisers can see or buy parts of it long after you have forgotten the activity.
why_wrong: Disk usage measures storage on one machine and says nothing about your online trail.
The count of connected devices is a fact about your network, not a record of your activity.
Screen size is a hardware detail with no bearing on what you leave behind online.

questions.q: Cyber ethics is best described as:
options: The technique of scrambling data so that it cannot be read in transit
The study of how computer hardware is manufactured
The moral principles that guide honest and respectful behaviour when using computers and the internet
The set of rules that decides how fast an internet connection must be
questions.explain: Cyber ethics is about how you ought to behave online: respecting other people's privacy and work, being truthful about what you share, and not causing harm through a screen. It guides conduct even where no law or technical control stops you.
why_wrong: That describes encryption, a technical safeguard rather than a question of conduct.
Hardware manufacturing is an engineering subject and has nothing to do with online behaviour.
Connection speed is a service matter decided by the provider, not an ethical principle.

questions.q: Plagiarism means:
options: Quoting a source and naming the author who wrote it
Presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own without crediting the source
Reading several sources before writing an assignment in your own words
Summarising a source in your own words and giving a proper citation
questions.explain: Plagiarism is a claim of authorship you are not entitled to make. It is the missing credit, not the act of using a source, that makes it wrong, so material taken from anywhere must be attributed even when it is free to read online.
why_wrong: Quoting with the author named is exactly the honest way to use a source.
Reading widely and then writing in your own words is normal, acceptable study.
A summary in your own words with a citation credits the source properly and is not plagiarism.

questions.q: Downloading a paid film or a paid program from an unauthorised site instead of buying it is an example of:
options: Phishing
Cyberbullying
Piracy, which infringes the owner's copyright
A brute force attack
questions.explain: Piracy is the unauthorised copying or distribution of work that someone else owns the rights to. Besides being unfair to the creator, such downloads are a common carrier of malware, because the file is supplied by a site with no accountability.
why_wrong: Phishing tricks a person into revealing sensitive information; no deception of that kind is involved here.
Cyberbullying is directed at harming a particular person online.
A brute force attack guesses passwords by trying every combination and has nothing to do with downloading content.

questions.q: Cyberbullying is best described as:
options: Using messages, posts or other online means to repeatedly harass, threaten or humiliate a person
Sending the same advertisement to a very large list of addresses
Copying a classmate's assignment and submitting it as your own
Leaving an honest negative review of a product you actually bought
questions.explain: Cyberbullying is harassment carried out through digital channels, and it is defined by its target and its repetition rather than by the platform used. It is especially damaging because the messages follow the victim home and can be seen by a large audience.
why_wrong: That is spam: unwanted bulk advertising, which is a nuisance rather than an attack on one person.
That is plagiarism, a matter of academic dishonesty rather than harassment.
An honest account of your own experience with a product is legitimate feedback, however unfavourable it is.

questions.q: Why is it important to install operating system and application updates soon after they are released?
options: They increase the amount of storage space available on the disk
They make the internet connection faster
They remove the need to use a password
They repair security flaws that attackers could otherwise exploit
questions.explain: Many updates close weaknesses that have already become public knowledge, and attackers deliberately target machines that have not applied them yet. Installing promptly shrinks the window during which a known flaw can be used against you.
why_wrong: Updates usually consume a little more disk space rather than creating extra.
Connection speed depends on the network and the provider, not on the software version you run.
Updates never replace authentication; you still sign in exactly as before.

questions.q: The main purpose of keeping regular backups of your files is:
options: To stop anyone else from being able to read the files
To be able to restore the files if they are lost, damaged or locked by ransomware
To make the computer start up faster
To prevent malware from ever reaching the computer
questions.explain: A backup is a second copy kept somewhere else, so that a failed disk, a deleted folder, a stolen laptop or a ransomware attack costs you time rather than your work. Keeping at least one copy offline matters, because malware can reach copies that stay permanently connected.
why_wrong: Keeping others from reading files is the job of encryption and access permissions, not of copying them.
Startup speed depends on the system and its hardware and is unaffected by the existence of copies.
A backup does not block an infection; it is what lets you recover after one.

questions.q: Which option correctly pairs these two version control systems with their type?
options: Git and Subversion (SVN) are both centralized
Git is distributed, while Subversion (SVN) is centralized
Git is centralized, while Subversion (SVN) is distributed
Git and Subversion (SVN) are both distributed
questions.explain: The type of a system is decided by where the history lives. Subversion keeps the full history on one central server, so every operation needs that server. Git is distributed: each person who clones a repository holds a complete copy of the history, which is why commits and log reading work without a network connection.
why_wrong: Git is not centralized; a Git clone carries the whole history, so no single server holds the only copy.
This reverses both systems: Git is the distributed one and Subversion is the centralized one.
Subversion is not distributed; a working copy taken from an SVN server holds the current files, not the project's whole history.

questions.q: What is the correct order of steps for contributing a change to a public GitHub project that you have no write access to?
options: Clone the original repository, commit and push your change to it, then fork it
Open a pull request first, then fork the repository and push the change into it
Fork the repository, clone your fork, commit and push your change, then open a pull request
Fork the repository, open an issue describing the change, then merge the change into the original project yourself
questions.explain: Without write access you cannot push into someone else's repository, so you first make a copy you do own by forking it. You clone that fork, make and push your commits there, and then a pull request asks the original owner to pull your finished work in. The owner reviews it and decides whether to merge.
why_wrong: Pushing to the original repository is exactly what is impossible without write access, and forking afterwards would not help.
A pull request compares work that already exists in a fork or branch, so there is nothing to propose until the change has been committed and pushed.
Opening an issue only reports or discusses something, and merging into the original project is the owner's decision, not yours.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT true of git commit?
options: It records the author's name and email along with the change
It stores the staged changes as a snapshot in the local repository
It sends the change to the remote repository on GitHub
It attaches a message describing what the change was
questions.explain: A commit is a purely local operation: it writes a snapshot of whatever was staged into the repository inside your own .git folder, together with the author identity, the time and your message. Nothing travels over the network until you run git push. This is why work can be committed with no internet connection at all.
why_wrong: A commit does record the configured author name and email, which is why git config user.name and user.email must be set before you begin.
Storing the staged changes as a snapshot in the local repository is precisely what a commit does.
The -m option exists to attach a message, and every commit carries one.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes forking a repository from cloning it?
options: Forking downloads the repository onto your computer, while cloning makes a copy under your account on GitHub
Both create a copy on GitHub, but forking copies fewer branches than cloning
Forking replaces the original repository with your own copy
Forking makes a copy of a repository under your own account on GitHub, while cloning downloads a repository onto your computer
questions.explain: Forking happens on the hosting site: GitHub creates a second repository, owned by you, linked to the original. Cloning happens between the server and your machine: it brings a repository down to your local disk so you can work on it. The usual contribution route uses both, forking first and then cloning the fork.
why_wrong: This reverses the two: downloading to your computer is cloning, and the copy under your account is the fork.
Cloning does not create anything on GitHub, and a fork does not leave branches out.
The original repository is untouched by a fork; its owner keeps it exactly as it was.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the difference between git branch feature and git checkout feature?
options: git branch feature creates a branch named feature, while git checkout feature switches your working directory over to that branch
git branch feature switches to the branch, while git checkout feature creates it
Both commands create the branch, but only git checkout also commits your current changes
git branch feature merges feature into the current branch, while git checkout feature deletes it
questions.explain: Creating a branch and moving onto it are two separate actions in Git. git branch feature only makes the new branch label; you stay where you are. git checkout feature moves you onto it, so that your next commits are recorded there.
why_wrong: This reverses the two commands: creation is done by git branch and switching by git checkout.
git checkout never commits anything; commits are made only by git commit.
Merging is done by git merge and deleting a branch by git branch -d, so neither description fits.

questions.q: Which statement about the hidden .git folder is correct?
options: It holds only the most recent version of each file, with the older versions kept on GitHub
It is created when a repository is initialised or cloned, and it holds the project's history and repository settings
You create it by hand and copy into it the files you want Git to track
It is the place where Git stores the files listed in .gitignore
questions.explain: The .git folder is the repository itself; everything outside it is just your working copy of the files. Git creates it for you when you run git init or git clone, and inside it Git keeps the commits, branches and configuration for that project. Deleting that folder would leave the files but throw away the entire history.
why_wrong: The whole history is stored locally inside .git, which is why you can read the log and check out old versions with no network.
Git creates the folder itself, and files are tracked by running git add, not by copying them into .git.
Files listed in .gitignore are deliberately left untracked, so Git does not store them anywhere.

questions.q: Why does Git provide a staging area between the working directory and the repository?
options: So that the changes are backed up on the remote server before they are committed
So that Git can check the code for errors before allowing a commit
So that teammates can review each change before it is committed
So that you can choose exactly which of your current changes go into the next commit, instead of committing everything you have edited
questions.explain: The staging area lets you build up a commit deliberately. If you have edited five files but only two of them belong to the bug fix you want to record, you stage just those two with git add and commit them, leaving the rest for a later commit. This is what keeps each commit a single, meaningful change.
why_wrong: The staging area is entirely local; nothing reaches a remote server until git push.
Git does not inspect or validate your code at any point, staging included.
Review by teammates happens after work is pushed, through a pull request, not in your own staging area.

questions.q: Which of the following is a feature of GitHub rather than of Git itself?
options: Recording a commit while your computer is offline
Opening a pull request to propose your changes to a project
Creating a branch in a local repository
Viewing past commits with git log
questions.explain: Git is the version control software on your machine; GitHub is a hosting website built around it that adds collaboration features. Pull requests, issues and forks belong to the website, not to the Git program. Commits, branches and the log are Git features and work with no account or internet connection at all.
why_wrong: Committing offline is the clearest sign of a Git feature, since the whole repository is on your own disk.
Branches are a core part of Git and can be created in a repository that was never put online.
git log is a Git command reading history stored locally in .git.

questions.q: Which command lets you check the settings Git is currently using, such as the configured user name and email?
options: git config --list
git status
git --version
git log --author
questions.explain: git config --list prints the configuration values in effect for the current repository, combining the system, global and local settings. It is the quick way to confirm that the identity you set earlier is the one Git will actually record. Setting a value and listing the values are done with the same config command, which is why the names look similar.
why_wrong: git status reports which files are modified, staged or untracked; it says nothing about configuration.
git --version reports which version of the Git program is installed, which is how you confirm the installation worked.
git log --author filters the commit history by a given author; it reads past commits rather than your settings.

questions.q: Which situation produces a merge conflict that Git cannot resolve on its own?
options: The two branches changed different files in the project
One branch has more commits on it than the other
Both branches being merged changed the same lines of the same file in different ways
One branch added a new file that the other branch does not contain
questions.explain: Git merges automatically whenever it can work out how to combine two sets of changes. It only stops when two branches have altered the very same lines of a file in incompatible ways, because then no rule can decide which version is meant. At that point Git marks the conflicting section and leaves the choice to a person.
why_wrong: Changes in different files do not overlap, so Git combines them without any difficulty.
The number of commits on each side is irrelevant; only overlapping edits cause a conflict.
A file added on one side only is simply brought into the merge; there is nothing competing with it.

questions.q: Which pair contains only malware types that do NOT make copies of themselves in order to spread?
options: Virus and worm
Worm and spyware
Virus and ransomware
Trojan horse and adware
questions.explain: Self-replication is what separates viruses and worms from the rest. A Trojan horse arrives because the user is persuaded to install it, and adware usually arrives bundled with some free program the user chose; neither reproduces itself to reach new machines. Every other pair listed contains one of the two replicating types.
why_wrong: Both replicate: a virus copies itself into host files and a worm copies itself across the network.
A worm is a self-replicating type, so this pair fails even though spyware does not replicate.
A virus is a self-replicating type, so this pair fails even though ransomware usually is not.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a Trojan horse from a virus?
options: A Trojan horse copies itself across a network on its own, while a virus needs a host program
A Trojan horse encrypts files and demands payment, while a virus displays advertisements
A Trojan horse relies on the user being tricked into installing it and does not copy itself, while a virus attaches to a host file and spreads when that file is run
A Trojan horse hides other malware from security software, while a virus only slows the machine down
questions.explain: A Trojan horse gets in by deception rather than by reproduction: it pretends to be something the user wants, and the user installs it. A virus does reproduce, but only by attaching itself to a file or program, so it travels wherever that infected file is copied and runs when the file is opened. The difference is disguise versus self-copying.
why_wrong: Spreading across a network on its own describes a worm, not a Trojan horse.
Encrypting files for payment is ransomware and displaying advertisements is adware; neither describes these two types.
Hiding other malware from security software is the work of a rootkit, and a virus does far more than slow a machine down.

questions.q: Which statement about antivirus software is correct?
options: Once installed it never needs updating, because it blocks all malware by design
It must be kept updated, because new malware appears constantly and an out-of-date antivirus will not recognise it
It removes the need for backups, since any infected file can always be repaired
It protects the computer only while the machine is disconnected from the internet
questions.explain: Antivirus software recognises threats from information about malware that is already known, and new malware is written every day. Updates refresh that knowledge, so protection is only as current as the last update. This is also why antivirus alone is not enough, and why backups and careful downloading habits still matter.
why_wrong: No antivirus blocks everything, and one that is never updated falls behind very quickly.
Files encrypted by ransomware or badly damaged by an infection often cannot be repaired, which is exactly why backups are kept.
Protection is most needed while online; antivirus runs regardless of the connection.

questions.q: Which option correctly pairs a malware type with its main purpose?
options: Adware - encrypting the victim's files and demanding a payment for the key
Spyware - flooding a website with traffic from thousands of machines at once
Rootkit - displaying unwanted advertisements in order to earn advertising revenue
Ransomware - extorting money by making the victim's files unusable until a payment is made
questions.explain: Each type of malware is defined by what the attacker is trying to achieve. Ransomware's goal is direct extortion: the files are encrypted or the system locked, and access is sold back to the owner. Adware chases advertising revenue, spyware chases information, and a rootkit chases hidden, privileged control.
why_wrong: Encrypting files for a payment is ransomware; adware's aim is advertising revenue.
Flooding a website with traffic from many machines is what a botnet is used for; spyware quietly gathers information instead.
Displaying unwanted advertisements is adware; a rootkit hides itself and gives the attacker administrator-level control.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a rootkit from spyware?
options: A rootkit collects passwords and browsing habits, while spyware hides other programs from the antivirus
A rootkit gives an attacker administrator-level control and conceals its own presence, while spyware exists to collect the user's information and pass it to someone else
A rootkit spreads across a network by itself, while spyware attaches itself to a host file
A rootkit locks files until a ransom is paid, while spyware fills the screen with advertisements
questions.explain: A rootkit is about control and concealment: it burrows into the system with high privileges and hides itself, and often other malware too, from the user and from security tools. Spyware is about surveillance: it watches what the user does and reports it back. Both are quiet, but for different reasons.
why_wrong: This reverses the two: collecting passwords and habits is spyware, and hiding programs from the antivirus is the rootkit.
Spreading across a network alone describes a worm, and attaching to a host file describes a virus.
Locking files for a ransom is ransomware, and filling the screen with advertisements is adware.

questions.q: Which of the following would NOT help protect a computer against malware?
