options: Installing operating system and application updates as soon as they are released
Doing everyday work from a standard user account rather than an administrator account
Switching the antivirus off so that the machine runs faster
Downloading software only from the maker's official website or an official app store
questions.explain: Turning the antivirus off removes a layer of protection for a small gain in speed, leaving the machine open to threats it would otherwise have caught. The other three are standard defences: updates close known weaknesses, a standard account limits what any malware that does run can reach, and trusted download sources cut off the commonest delivery route.
why_wrong: Prompt updating closes the known weaknesses that worms and other malware exploit.
Malware running in a standard account inherits only that account's limited rights, so it can do less damage.
Official sources give you the software the maker actually published, rather than an altered copy.

questions.q: Why is paying the ransom generally discouraged as a response to a ransomware attack?
options: Because ransomware removes itself after a few days, so the files come back on their own
Because antivirus software can reverse any ransomware encryption once it is installed
Because the ransom message is only a warning and no files are actually encrypted
Because there is no guarantee the attacker will restore the files, and the payment funds and encourages further attacks
questions.explain: The victim is dealing with a criminal, so the promise of a decryption key is worth nothing; many who pay get nothing back or are asked for more. Payment also proves the business model works and pays for the next round of attacks. This is why offline backups that have been tested are treated as the real answer to ransomware.
why_wrong: Encrypted files stay encrypted; nothing expires or reverses itself with time.
Antivirus may remove the malware, but it cannot undo strong encryption without the key.
The encryption is real, which is exactly what makes the demand effective.

questions.q: What do all social-engineering attacks have in common, whatever technique is used?
options: They target the people who use a system, relying on trust, fear or helpfulness rather than on a flaw in the software
They require the attacker to install malware on the victim's computer before anything else can happen
They are always delivered by email, which is why email filtering stops them
They only succeed against users who are logged in with administrator rights
questions.explain: Social engineering is an attack on the human being rather than on the machine. Whether the attacker phones, emails, leaves a USB drive or follows someone through a door, the method is to persuade a person to hand over information or perform an unsafe action. That is why technical defences alone cannot stop it and why awareness training matters.
why_wrong: Malware is one possible outcome of a successful trick, not a requirement; pretexting or shoulder surfing can succeed without any malicious program at all.
Email is only one channel; phone calls, text messages, physical entry and face-to-face conversation are all used, so email filtering covers only part of the problem.
Ordinary users are targeted constantly, because their accounts, money and personal details are worth taking even without administrator rights.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three standard categories of authentication factors?
options: Something you know
Something you have
Something you are
Something you share
questions.explain: Authentication factors are grouped into three categories: something you know (a password or PIN), something you have (a phone, a card, a security key) and something you are (a fingerprint, a face or an iris). Multi-factor authentication means combining factors from different categories, so that stealing one does not give access. Anything deliberately shared is the opposite of a secret and therefore proves nothing about who you are.
why_wrong: This is a real category: passwords, PINs and security answers all belong to it.
This is a real category: one-time codes on a registered phone, smart cards and hardware keys belong to it.
This is a real category: biometrics such as fingerprint and face recognition belong to it.

questions.q: Which of the following does private or incognito browsing NOT do?
options: Hide your activity from the network you are using and from the websites you visit
Keep the pages you visit out of the browser's saved history on that device
Discard the cookies created during the session when the private window is closed
Keep the session separate from accounts you are already signed into in an ordinary window
questions.explain: Private browsing is about what is left behind on the device, not about anonymity on the network. The sites you open, your college network, your internet provider and your employer can all still see the traffic, because the browser is only choosing not to save local records. Treating incognito mode as protection on an untrusted network is a common and risky misunderstanding.
why_wrong: Private mode really does leave the visited pages out of the local history, which is one of its genuine purposes.
Cookies created in a private session really are thrown away when the window is closed, so sites do not remember the visit locally.
A private window really does start without the sign-in state of the normal window, which is why it is handy for a second account.

questions.q: What distinguishes a quid pro quo attack from baiting?
options: In quid pro quo the attacker offers a service or help in return for information or access, while baiting relies on a tempting item the victim picks up or downloads
In quid pro quo the attacker uses a phone, while baiting is always done by email
In quid pro quo the victim is threatened, while in baiting the victim is flattered
In quid pro quo malware is installed, while baiting never involves any software
questions.explain: Both techniques exploit the appeal of getting something, but the shape of the offer differs. Quid pro quo means "something for something": the attacker poses as helpful support staff and offers to fix a problem in exchange for a password or remote access. Baiting instead leaves out temptation such as a labelled USB drive or a free-download link and waits for curiosity to do the rest.
why_wrong: The channel is not what separates them; a quid pro quo offer can arrive by email or chat, and bait can be a physical object left in a corridor.
Neither technique is defined by threat or flattery; both work by offering something the victim wants.
Baiting very often delivers malware, for example through the dropped USB drive or the pirated download, so this is not a dividing line.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes authentication from authorisation?
options: Authentication establishes who you are; authorisation decides what you are allowed to do once your identity is known
Authentication decides what you are allowed to do; authorisation proves who you are
Authentication applies only to administrators, while authorisation applies only to ordinary users
Authentication is the encryption of your password, while authorisation is the encryption of your files
questions.explain: The two steps happen in that order. First the system checks your identity from a password, a code or a fingerprint, and only after that does it consult its rules to decide which files and actions that identity may reach. This separation is why two people who both log in successfully can still see very different things.
why_wrong: This reverses the two terms; proving identity is authentication, and granting permissions is authorisation.
Both apply to every account; a standard user is authenticated at login and then authorised to do only a limited set of things.
Neither term means encryption; encryption is a separate control that scrambles data so it cannot be read.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT part of a person's digital footprint?
options: A handwritten diary kept in a locked drawer at home
A post that was deleted from a social media account last year
A record of visited pages collected by cookies in a browser
A comment left under a publicly visible video
questions.explain: A digital footprint is the trail of data a person leaves through their use of digital services, whether they created it deliberately or a system recorded it in the background. Deleted posts still count, because copies may survive in caches, backups and screenshots. Something written on paper and never digitised is simply not part of that trail.
why_wrong: A deleted post is still part of the footprint, since removal from your own view does not remove copies held elsewhere.
Records gathered by cookies are the classic example of a passive digital footprint.
A public comment is an active digital footprint, created deliberately by the user.

questions.q: Which option pairs a phishing variant with the channel it actually uses?
options: Smishing - text messages sent to a mobile phone
Vishing - comments posted on social media profiles
Whaling - a printed letter delivered by post
Clone phishing - a live phone call in which the attacker reads a script
questions.explain: The names of the phishing variants describe either the channel or the target. Smishing comes from SMS, so it travels by text message; vishing comes from voice and travels by phone call; whaling names the size of the target, a senior figure, and usually arrives by email. Clone phishing names the method, copying a genuine message the victim has already received and swapping in a malicious link or attachment.
why_wrong: Vishing is phishing by voice call, not by social media posts.
Whaling describes a phishing attack aimed at a senior figure such as a CEO, and it is normally delivered electronically rather than on paper.
A live scripted phone call is vishing; clone phishing is a copied version of a genuine message the victim received earlier.

questions.q: Downloading a paid film or paid software from an unauthorised site instead of buying it is best described as:
options: Piracy, a breach of the copyright held by the creator or publisher
Plagiarism, because the work was made by somebody else
Phishing, because the site is not the official one
A passive digital footprint, because the download happens in the background
questions.explain: Copying and distributing protected work without permission is piracy, and it infringes the owner's copyright whether or not any money changes hands. The wrong done is taking a copy that the creator had the exclusive right to supply. It is different from passing off someone's work as your own, which is a separate offence.
why_wrong: Plagiarism means presenting another person's work as your own; the downloader is not claiming to have made the film or the software.
Phishing means tricking a person into handing over credentials or details; here the user is the one seeking out the site.
A passive footprint is data collected about you without deliberate action; deliberately downloading a file is an active choice, and the term describes tracking rather than legality.

questions.q: How does a phishing email differ from ordinary spam?
options: Phishing tries to trick the reader into giving up credentials or details or into running something harmful, while spam is unsolicited bulk advertising
Phishing is sent in bulk, while spam is always sent to one carefully chosen person
Phishing always carries an attachment, while spam never does
Phishing arrives only from unknown senders, while spam comes only from known contacts
questions.explain: The dividing line is intent. Spam is unwanted advertising, annoying but usually just trying to sell something. Phishing is an attack: the message is designed to make you reveal a password, card number or one-time code, or to open something that infects the machine, and it often disguises itself as a message from an organisation you trust.
why_wrong: Both can be sent in bulk; bulk delivery is typical of spam and of ordinary phishing alike, while targeting one person is spear phishing.
Many phishing messages carry no attachment at all and rely entirely on a link to a fake login page.
Either kind can appear to come from a familiar name, since sender addresses are easy to forge or imitate.

questions.q: Locking an account after a small number of consecutive failed login attempts is aimed most directly at which threat?
options: Automated guessing of the password by trying one combination after another
Somebody watching over your shoulder as you type the password
A phishing page that persuades you to type the password yourself
A firewall rule that has been configured incorrectly
questions.explain: Guessing attacks depend on being allowed a very large number of attempts. A lockout, or a growing delay between tries, removes that freedom, so even a weak password cannot be worked out by sheer repetition. It does nothing about attacks where the attacker already has the correct password.
why_wrong: Shoulder surfing gives the attacker the correct password on the first try, so a lockout for failed attempts never triggers.
A phishing victim hands over the correct password, which means the attacker logs in successfully rather than failing repeatedly.
Firewall configuration governs network traffic and is unrelated to how many login attempts an account allows.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs an online behaviour with the correct term for it?
options: Sending unsolicited bulk advertising messages to large numbers of people - spamming
Submitting someone else's writing as your own in an assignment - piracy
Repeatedly posting hurtful messages aimed at one person - plagiarism
Copying a paid game from an unauthorised download site - cyberbullying
questions.explain: These terms name different wrongs and are easy to mix up. Spamming is flooding people with unwanted bulk messages; plagiarism is presenting another person's work as your own; cyberbullying is repeated online behaviour intended to harass or humiliate a person; piracy is copying protected work without permission. Using the right term matters because the remedies and the rules that apply are different in each case.
why_wrong: Passing off another person's writing as your own is plagiarism; piracy is unauthorised copying of protected work such as films or software.
Repeated hurtful messages directed at a person are cyberbullying, not plagiarism.
Copying a paid game from an unauthorised site is piracy; cyberbullying involves harassing a person.

questions.q: Phishing messages very often warn that an account will be blocked within a few hours unless you act at once. What is the main purpose of that urgency?
options: To push the reader into acting before there is time to stop, check the sender and verify the claim
To make the message pass through spam filters that give priority to time-limited mail
To satisfy a rule that requires email about accounts to state a deadline
To make the attacker's link work faster than an ordinary link would
questions.explain: Urgency is a deliberate psychological lever. A reader who feels a deadline is about to expire reacts rather than reflects, and skips the very checks, such as looking at the real sender address or ringing the organisation, that would expose the fraud. Recognising manufactured pressure as a warning sign in itself is one of the most reliable defences.
why_wrong: Spam filters do not favour messages that mention deadlines; urgent wording is often treated as a suspicious signal instead.
No rule requires deadlines in messages about accounts, and genuine organisations rarely demand action within hours.
The wording of a message has no effect on how quickly a link loads.

questions.q: A personal firewall rule that stops a program on your own computer from sending data out to the internet is an example of:
options: Outbound traffic filtering
Inbound traffic filtering
Signature-based virus scanning
Encryption of the connection
questions.explain: Firewalls work in both directions. Inbound filtering controls what may reach your machine from outside, while outbound filtering controls what your machine is allowed to send out. Blocking outbound connections is useful because it can cut off a program that is quietly trying to contact an attacker's server.
why_wrong: Inbound filtering governs connections coming in from the network towards your machine, which is the opposite direction.
Signature scanning compares files against known malware patterns and is the work of antivirus software, not a firewall rule.
Encryption scrambles the contents of traffic; the rule described here blocks the traffic rather than protecting its contents.

questions.q: Why does installing operating system and application updates promptly count as a security practice rather than just a convenience?
options: Updates commonly repair known security flaws, and those flaws are public knowledge that attackers already know how to exploit
Updates free up storage space by deleting old files from the device
Updates remove the need to run antivirus software or a firewall
Updates replace your existing passwords with stronger ones automatically
questions.explain: When a vendor publishes a security fix, the weakness it repairs becomes widely known, and unpatched machines become easy targets. Applying the update closes the hole before it can be used against you. This is why timing matters: the risk is highest in the gap between the fix being released and it being installed.
why_wrong: Updates frequently use more space rather than less, and freeing storage is not their purpose.
Patching, antivirus and firewalls address different problems, so an update never makes the others unnecessary.
Updates change software, not your account passwords; changing a password is always your own action.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a form of phishing?
options: Tailgating
Smishing
Vishing
Whaling
questions.explain: Phishing means sending a deceptive message that imitates a trusted source, and its variants are named after the channel or the target: smishing by SMS, vishing by voice call, whaling aimed at a senior figure. Tailgating is also social engineering, but it is physical, walking in behind someone who has legitimately opened a secure door. It involves no fraudulent message at all.
why_wrong: Smishing is phishing delivered by text message.
Vishing is phishing delivered by a voice call.
Whaling is a phishing attack aimed at a senior person such as a chief executive.

questions.q: Which option correctly matches a security control with the problem it mainly addresses?
options: Multi-factor authentication - it keeps an attacker out even when the password has been stolen
A firewall - it removes virus-infected files already stored on the hard disk
The principle of least privilege - it makes passwords harder to guess
A password manager - it encrypts the network traffic between the browser and a website
questions.explain: Each control is designed for a particular problem, and matching them correctly is what makes a sensible set of defences. A second factor matters precisely in the case where the first factor has failed, because the attacker who knows the password still lacks the phone or the key. Firewalls filter network traffic, least privilege limits the damage an account or program can do, and a password manager stores strong unique secrets.
why_wrong: A firewall filters traffic according to rules; cleaning infected files stored on disk is the work of antivirus software.
Least privilege limits what an account or program is allowed to do, so it limits damage; it has no effect on how guessable a password is.
A password manager generates and stores passwords; the encryption of traffic in transit is provided by HTTPS.

questions.q: On a shared computer, why is logging out of an account better than simply closing the browser tab?
options: Closing the tab can leave the session active, so the next person may reopen the site and still be signed in
Closing a tab deletes the account's password from the website's server
Logging out encrypts every file that was downloaded during the session
Logging out stops the website from ever placing cookies on that computer
questions.explain: Being signed in is a state stored in a cookie or token, and closing a tab does not necessarily end it. Logging out tells the site to end the session, so the credential left behind on the machine is no longer usable. On a shared or public computer that difference decides whether the next user finds your account open.
why_wrong: Nothing a browser does removes a password from the website's server, and passwords are not stored in the tab.
Logging out ends a session; it performs no encryption of downloaded files, which remain on the disk as they were.
Cookies are set while you use the site; logging out invalidates the session rather than preventing cookies from existing.

questions.q: An email claiming to be from a bank asks you to confirm your account details. Which sequence of steps is the correct way to handle it?
options: Do not click anything; check the sender's full address and hover over the links; contact the bank on a number you already have; then report and delete the message
Click the link first to see where it leads; if the page looks wrong, close it; then delete the message
Reply to the message asking the sender to prove they are genuine; wait for the answer; then decide whether to click the link
Forward it to friends so they can warn you if it is fake; if nobody objects, enter the details
questions.explain: The safe order puts every check before any action that could cost you something. Inspecting the real sender address and the true destination of a link risks nothing, while verification through a number or address you already possess bypasses anything the attacker supplied. Reporting and deleting at the end protects other people without leaving the message lying around to be clicked later.
why_wrong: Opening the link is the very action the attacker wants; a convincing fake page or an automatic download can do damage before you judge it.
A reply reaches the attacker, confirms that your address is live and invites a more convincing follow-up; a criminal will happily claim to be genuine.
Forwarding spreads the attack, and the silence of friends is no evidence of safety; entering the details is exactly the outcome the attacker wanted.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the difference between using sudo and logging in as root?
options: sudo raises privileges for a single command while the user works normally the rest of the time, whereas a root login gives every command in the session full privileges
sudo grants fewer rights than root, so system files can never be modified through it
sudo runs a command without recording it, while every root login is written to a log
sudo is the Windows name for the same thing that Linux calls the root account
questions.explain: Both reach administrator-level power, but they differ in how long that power lasts. With sudo the elevation is attached to one command, so an ordinary mistake or a malicious program running the rest of the time is still confined to a normal account. Staying logged in as root removes that safety net for everything you do, which is why it goes against the principle of least privilege.
why_wrong: A command run through sudo has full administrative rights and can modify system files; the limit is on duration, not on power.
Commands run through sudo are normally logged, so this reverses the usual position.
sudo is a Linux and Unix command, not a Windows term, and root is an account rather than a command.

questions.q: Why is installing an app from an official app store safer than installing it from a link sent in a message?
options: Apps in an official store are reviewed and digitally signed, and updates or removals reach you through the same controlled channel
Apps in an official store are always free, so nobody has a motive to attack their users
An official store guarantees that an installed app can never request any permissions
Apps installed from a store are never allowed to use the internet
questions.explain: The value of an official store is the checks around the app rather than the app alone. Submissions are screened and signed, so the copy you receive is the one the developer published, and if a harmful app is later discovered the store can push an update or pull it from devices. A file from a random link comes with none of that and may be a modified or repackaged version.
why_wrong: Official stores are full of paid apps, and attackers target the users of free apps just as readily.
Apps from a store still request permissions; the store shows you what is requested, and it remains your decision whether to grant it.
Store apps use the internet normally; installation source does not determine network access.

questions.q: In the link http://www.yourbank.secure-login-verify.com/update, which part decides which website you actually reach?
options: secure-login-verify.com, the registered domain that sits immediately before the first single slash
yourbank, because it is the recognisable name that appears earliest in the address
update, the word that comes after the last slash
www, which always identifies the organisation that owns the site
questions.explain: A web address is read from the right-hand end of the host name, not the left. The registered domain is the last two labels before the first single slash, and everything placed before it is merely a subdomain the owner of that domain can name as they like. Attackers exploit this by putting a trusted name at the front, so the habit worth building is to look at the end of the host name rather than the beginning.
why_wrong: A familiar word at the front is only a subdomain chosen by whoever owns the real domain, so it proves nothing about ownership.
The path after the slash is chosen by the same site and merely names a page on it; it cannot change which server you reach.
www is just a common subdomain label and can be attached to any domain at all.

questions.q: Every time Bhavya runs git status in her project she has to scroll past hundreds of entries from a build folder and a folder of downloaded libraries that she never wants stored in the project's history. She is also afraid of sweeping them in by accident with git add . one day. What is the proper fix?
options: Create a file listing those folder names so Git stops treating their contents as files to track
Delete the two folders before every commit and rebuild them again afterwards
Commit the two folders once, so that Git stops reporting them as untracked
Stop using git add . and name every wanted file by hand from now on
questions.explain: Git needs to be told which paths are generated or downloaded rather than authored, and a .gitignore file in the repository does exactly that: the patterns listed there are skipped, so those paths stop appearing as untracked and cannot be staged by accident. The history then contains only the files a human actually wrote, which is what makes it useful to read. This is also the standard protection against committing files that hold passwords or keys.
why_wrong: Deleting and rebuilding generated folders by hand wastes time and risks losing something she needs, and the folders reappear as untracked the moment she rebuilds.
Committing them puts the very content she wanted excluded into the history permanently, and every rebuild would then show them as modified.
Naming each file by hand is slow and error prone, and it does nothing about the hundreds of lines of noise in git status, which is otherwise a useful report.

questions.q: Aarav spent the afternoon making small edits across four files and can no longer remember exactly what he altered. Before he marks anything for his next commit, he wants to see the actual lines that are different from the last recorded snapshot. Which command should he run?
options: git status
git log
git diff
git branch
questions.explain: git diff prints the line-by-line difference between the files as they stand in the working directory and the version Git has recorded, with removed lines and added lines shown separately. That is exactly the review to do just before staging, because it shows the content of the change rather than merely the names of the files involved. It only reads, so running it can change nothing.
why_wrong: git status tells him which files are new, modified or staged, but it never shows what changed inside a file.
git log lists the commits that were already recorded, with their authors and messages, not the edits he has not committed yet.
git branch lists the branches that exist in the repository and says nothing about file contents.

questions.q: Tanvi has finished a photo gallery on a branch called gallery, and that work must now become part of the project's main line. She is currently standing on the gallery branch. What should she do?
options: Run git merge main while she is still on gallery
Switch to main first, and then run git merge gallery
Run git merge gallery while she is still on gallery
Delete the main branch, so that gallery becomes the main line
questions.explain: A merge always brings the branch you name into the branch you are currently standing on, so the direction is decided by where you are, not by what you intend. To get gallery's commits into main she must first move onto main and then merge gallery into it. Checking which branch you are on before merging is the habit that prevents merging the wrong way round.
why_wrong: Merging main into gallery updates her own branch with the shared work; it delivers nothing of hers to main.
Merging a branch into itself does nothing at all, because Git has no new commits to bring across.
Deleting main throws away the shared line of development that everyone else works from, and merging exists precisely so that this is never necessary.

questions.q: Farhan joins a project team on his first day. The project already lives in a repository on GitHub with two years of history, and he needs a full working copy on his laptop, history included, so he can start contributing. Which command does he run?
options: git init
git pull
git remote add origin <url>
git clone <url>
questions.explain: git clone copies an existing repository from a remote onto your own machine, bringing the working files and the complete history with it, and it records the address it came from as the remote named origin. Because Git is distributed, the copy on his laptop is a full repository in its own right, so he can commit and read the log without contacting the server. It is the standard first command for joining any existing project.
why_wrong: git init starts a brand new empty repository from a folder on his own machine, which is not what he needs when the project already exists on the server.
git pull updates a repository he already has, and there is nothing on his laptop yet for it to update.
Adding a remote only records a short name for a URL inside a repository that already exists, and it downloads nothing.

questions.q: Meenal commits her work and runs git push, but Git refuses it and reports that the remote contains commits she does not have on her machine. A teammate pushed to the same branch an hour ago. What should she do?
options: Run git init again to repair her repository, then push
Delete her local repository, clone it again and redo her work by hand
Run git pull to bring the teammate's commits into her branch, settle any conflict, and then push again
Keep repeating git push until one of the attempts succeeds
questions.explain: Git refuses a push that would leave the remote without commits it already has, which is a deliberate protection against wiping out a teammate's work. The cure is to bring their commits down and combine them with hers first, which is what git pull does, and only then to push the combined result. If both of them changed the same lines she will resolve a conflict in the middle of that, which is a normal part of working together.
why_wrong: git init starts a new repository and repairs nothing; hers is perfectly healthy and is simply behind the remote.
Re-cloning throws away the commits she has already made and forces her to redo work that Git is able to merge for her.
The refusal is a rule about history, not a network glitch, so repeating the identical push produces the identical refusal.

questions.q: Ayesha's first two commits on a newly set up laptop show an author name she does not recognise. Before changing anything, she wants to see exactly which identity settings Git is currently using. Which command shows her that?
options: git --version
git status
git config --list
git log --oneline
questions.explain: git config --list prints the settings currently in effect, including user.name and user.email, so she can see what Git will attach to her next commit and at which level it was set. Reading the configuration before changing it is sensible, because the value may be coming from a system-wide or global file rather than from this one project. Once she knows, she can set the correct value with git config.
why_wrong: git --version prints the version of Git that is installed and says nothing about configuration.
git status reports which files are new, modified or staged inside the repository.
git log --oneline shows the commits already recorded, so it reveals the name that was used but not which setting is configured now.

questions.q: Vikram's laptop is stolen the night before a deadline. He had pushed everything to GitHub that morning and made no commits afterwards, and two teammates have clones of the repository on their own machines. What has happened to the project's history?
options: All of it survives: the remote and each teammate's clone hold the complete history, so the project can simply be cloned again
Only the current files survive, because the history itself existed only on the stolen laptop
Only the commits each teammate personally made survive, since a clone stores just its owner's work
Nothing survives, because a repository stops working once the machine it was created on is gone
questions.explain: Cloning a Git repository copies the whole thing, every commit included, so each teammate's machine and the copy on GitHub are all complete repositories rather than partial snapshots. That redundancy is a natural consequence of Git being distributed, which is why people say that every clone is a backup. Vikram simply clones from the remote onto a new machine and carries on.
why_wrong: Keeping the history is the entire point of the repository, and a clone contains that history rather than only the latest files.
A clone holds every commit in the branch it copied, whoever wrote it, not only its owner's contributions.
A repository is not tied to the machine that created it; any complete copy can be cloned onward indefinitely.

questions.q: While fixing a bug in cart.js, Nidhi also made unrelated experimental edits to style.css that she is not happy with yet. She wants the next commit to contain the bug fix alone, without throwing away the CSS work. What should she do?
options: Run git add . and then commit, because Git records only the file mentioned in the commit message
Run git add cart.js and then commit, leaving the style.css edits sitting in her working directory
Undo the style.css edits, commit the fix, and retype the CSS afterwards
Commit both files now and write in the message that the CSS part should be ignored
questions.explain: The staging area exists so that a commit can contain a chosen subset of your changes rather than everything you happen to have touched. Staging only cart.js means the commit snapshot holds just the bug fix, while the style.css edits stay in the working directory, uncommitted and untouched, ready to be finished later. That is how a history of small, single-purpose commits is built.
why_wrong: git add . stages every change in the folder, and a commit message is only descriptive text: it has no power to exclude a file from the snapshot.
Discarding work she wants to keep is unnecessary, since Git can record one file and leave the other alone.
A message cannot un-record a change; the CSS edits would be a permanent part of that commit's snapshot whatever the text said.

questions.q: Ritu has write access to her team's repository on GitHub, but the team's rule is that nothing reaches the main branch until another member has read the change. She has finished a login page. What is the normal way to get it reviewed and then included?
options: Fork the repository to her personal account, because a pull request can only come from a fork
Push her work on a separate branch and open a pull request, so a teammate can review it before it is merged
Push straight to main and ask a teammate to read the code afterwards
Email the changed files to a teammate, who can paste them in if they approve
questions.explain: A pull request is GitHub's review mechanism: it proposes the commits on one branch for merging into another and shows the reviewer the exact line-by-line changes, with a place to comment on them. Because Ritu already has write access she can push her branch into the same repository, so no fork is involved. Nothing reaches main until the pull request is merged, which is precisely what the team's rule asks for.
why_wrong: Forking is the route for someone without write access; a pull request works just as well from a branch inside the same repository.
Pushing to main first defeats the rule, because the unreviewed code is already in the shared line of development.
Emailed files lose the commit history and the line-by-line view, and retyping or pasting them by hand invites mistakes.

questions.q: Ravi uses an open source library and finds that one of its functions crashes when given an empty input. He cannot write the fix himself, but he can describe exactly how to reproduce the crash. What is the appropriate way to tell the maintainers on GitHub?
options: Open a pull request on the repository containing no changes
Fork the repository, since a fork notifies the maintainers that something is wrong
Star the repository so that the maintainers look at it
Open an issue describing the crash and the steps that reproduce it
questions.explain: Issues are GitHub's tracker for bugs and tasks: each one is a numbered entry that stays with the repository and can be discussed, assigned and finally closed. A clear report with reproduction steps is a genuine contribution even without code, because it is what lets a maintainer see the failure for themselves. Many projects later link the fixing pull request to the issue it closes.
why_wrong: A pull request proposes specific changes to the code, so an empty one gives the maintainers nothing to review and does not describe the bug.
A fork simply gives him a personal copy of the project and tells the maintainers nothing at all.
Starring is a bookmark and a signal of appreciation; it carries no message and reports nothing.

questions.q: Two weeks ago Sneha committed report.tex, and she has committed many times since. Today she deletes that file by mistake and empties the recycle bin. Her project is a Git repository and all of that work was committed. What is her position?
options: The file is gone, because Git stores only the most recent version of a project
The file is gone, because deleting a file also removes it from every commit that contained it
The file is recoverable, because each commit is a stored snapshot and the version from an earlier commit can be brought back
The file is recoverable only if she had pushed it to GitHub, since local commits do not keep file contents
questions.explain: A commit is a permanent snapshot of the files as they were at that moment, and those snapshots live inside the repository in the .git folder. Deleting a file in the working directory is just another change to the current state; it does not rewrite the commits that already contain the file. Being able to return to any recorded state is the whole reason for keeping a project under version control.
why_wrong: Keeping every committed version rather than only the latest is the entire purpose of version control.
History is not rewritten by a later deletion; the commits that already hold the file are untouched by what she does today.
Local commits store the full content of the files on her own machine, which is exactly why Git works with no network at all.

questions.q: Ishan's lab computer has antivirus software installed, but the machine has been kept off the network and the software has received no updates for a year. It scans a file brought in on a pen drive, reports it as clean, and the file later turns out to be malicious. What best explains this?
options: Antivirus software scans only files that arrive over the internet, never files from removable media
Antivirus software stops working altogether once it is a year out of date
The scanner compares files against a database of known threats, and a year-old database does not know anything released since
A clean report proves a file is harmless, so the file cannot really have been malicious
questions.explain: Traditional scanning works by matching files against a constantly updated list of known malicious programs, so the protection is only as current as that list. A scanner whose database stopped a year ago is blind to everything created or discovered since, even though it still runs and still reports results. This is why keeping the antivirus definitions updated matters as much as having the software installed.
why_wrong: Antivirus software scans files wherever they come from, including pen drives, local disks and network shares.
An out-of-date product keeps running and keeps scanning; the limitation is what it knows about, not whether it works.
A clean result means only that nothing matched what the scanner currently knows, which is not the same as proof that a file is safe.

questions.q: Priyanka notices her hostel laptop behaving oddly: programs she does not recognise are running and the disk stays busy when she is doing nothing. The laptop is on the shared hostel network with a shared folder mounted. What is the sensible first step?
options: Keep it connected and carry on working, so she can watch whether the behaviour gets worse
Disconnect the laptop from the network, and then scan it with up-to-date security software
Copy her documents onto the shared folder at once so that they are safe
Change the password on the hostel router, which will clear the infection from her laptop
questions.explain: Taking a suspect machine off the network does two things immediately: it stops anything malicious from reaching other machines or shared folders, and it cuts the path by which her data could be sent out to an attacker. Once it is isolated, a scan with current definitions can look for what is actually there. Containing first and investigating second is the standard order for any suspected infection.
why_wrong: Staying connected gives the infection more time to spread across the shared network and to keep sending her data out.
Copying files from a possibly infected machine onto a shared folder risks carrying the infection to everyone else who uses it.
A router password controls who may join the network; it changes nothing about software already running on her laptop.

questions.q: Manav keeps a copy of all his work on an external hard disk that stays plugged into his desktop day and night. Malicious software encrypts his documents and demands payment, and he then finds that the copies on the external disk have been encrypted as well. What is the lesson about backups?
options: A backup copy must be kept disconnected, because anything the machine can write to can be encrypted along with it
External disks are unsuitable for backups, and only printed copies are truly safe
The backup failed because the disk was too small, so a larger disk would have survived
Backups are useless against this kind of attack, so paying is the only way out
questions.explain: Encrypting malware works through everything the infected machine can reach, and a permanently attached drive or a continuously synced folder is just another place it can write. A copy that spends its life unplugged, or is otherwise out of reach of the running system, is what survives the attack and lets him wipe the machine and restore. A backup is only proven when a restore from it has actually been tested.
why_wrong: External disks are perfectly good for backups; it was the permanent connection that exposed this one, and a disk stored unplugged would have been untouched.
Capacity had nothing to do with it, since the malware encrypted whatever files it could reach regardless of the size of the disk.
A disconnected copy would have let him recover without paying, and payment never guarantees that a working key arrives.

questions.q: Security software removes a program from Deepak's laptop that had been quietly recording everything he typed for the past month. The laptop now scans clean. What must he still do?
options: Nothing more, because removing the program undoes whatever it captured
Reinstall the same program from a different website so that it works properly
Change only the password of his laptop account, since that is the machine that was infected
Change the password of every account he signed into during that month, using a device he trusts
questions.explain: Removing the program stops any further capture, but it cannot recall what was already sent to whoever planted it, and a month of typing includes every password he entered. He should therefore treat all of those accounts as compromised and reset them from a device he is confident is clean, turning on multi-factor authentication where it is offered. Cleaning the machine and cleaning up the consequences are two separate jobs.
why_wrong: Deleting the program cannot take back the keystrokes it has already sent out, and those keystrokes include his passwords.
That program was the malware itself, so installing it again would simply reinfect the machine.
It recorded everything he typed, so every account he signed into is affected, not merely the local one.

questions.q: Karthik's internet provider warns that a device on his home connection is taking part in attacks on other websites. The only device he never touched after installing is a network camera that still uses the login printed in its manual and whose software he has never updated. What is happening, and what should he do?
options: The camera has been taken over and is being used, with many other machines, to send attack traffic; he should replace its default login and update its software
The camera cannot be responsible, because only computers and phones can be used in attacks
The camera is being used to show him advertisements, so clearing his browser will stop it
His provider has mistaken ordinary video traffic for an attack, so nothing needs to be done
questions.explain: Any internet-connected device with a processor can be infected and enrolled into a large group of remotely controlled machines, and devices left on their factory login with old software are the easiest to recruit. Their combined traffic is then aimed at a chosen target on the attacker's command, while each owner notices nothing. Giving the camera a unique password and installing its updates removes the way in.
why_wrong: Cameras, routers and other small networked devices run real software and are favourite targets precisely because they are rarely updated.
Advertising shown in a browser is an entirely different problem, and it would not direct traffic at somebody else's website.
A sustained stream of traffic aimed at one outside target is not what a camera streaming to its owner looks like.

questions.q: A print shop returns Ruchi's pen drive after printing her assignment. Plugged into her own laptop it shows her own files plus a folder shortcut and a setup file she never put there. What is the safe way to proceed?
options: Open the setup file to find out what it is, since one file cannot do much harm
Leave the unknown items unopened, scan the drive with up-to-date security software, and delete anything she did not put there
Copy everything from the drive onto her desktop first and decide afterwards
Rename the unfamiliar files, which stops them from being able to run
questions.explain: Removable media passed between machines is a classic carrier, and a shop computer used by hundreds of strangers is exactly where an infection gets picked up. Most of what could be on that drive needs one thing from her, namely that she opens or runs it, so the safe order is to scan first and never launch an unknown program. Unexpected shortcuts and setup files on a drive she did not create belong in the bin.
why_wrong: Running an unknown program is precisely the action such software needs from its victim, and a single program can install anything it likes.
Copying a suspect file onto her own disk moves the problem closer rather than removing it, and she would still have to decide what it is.
A different name does not change what a file contains; it will still do the same thing if it is opened.

questions.q: On results day the college website becomes unreachable. The technical team finds it is being buried under requests from tens of thousands of ordinary home computers and routers around the world, whose owners have no idea anything is happening. What is going on?
options: Each of those owners has personally decided to open the college website at the same moment
The website has been encrypted and held to ransom, which is why nobody can reach it
Those machines are infected and are being directed together by one attacker to flood the site with traffic
One extremely fast computer is producing all of that traffic and only appears to come from many places
questions.explain: A large collection of infected machines under a single remote controller can be pointed at one target so that their combined requests exhaust it, which is what makes the site unreachable for everyone else. The owners of those machines are victims too, and normally notice nothing, since each one contributes only a small share of the flood. Traffic coming from so many separate genuine addresses is also what makes such an attack hard to filter out.
why_wrong: Tens of thousands of strangers across the world do not coincidentally open one college's website, and the owners are unaware of the traffic their machines send.
Ransom malware makes a victim's own files unreadable and demands payment; it does not generate a flood of requests from other people's computers.
The scenario's defining feature is that the traffic really does originate on many separate infected machines, which is what gives the attack its scale.

questions.q: Aditya will not bother with security software or updates, saying his laptop holds nothing but films and lecture notes, so an infection would cost him nothing. Which reply is correct?
options: An infected machine is valuable in itself, since it can be used to attack others and it exposes every account he signs into from it
He is right, because malicious software only harms machines that store financial documents
He is right, as long as he never uses the laptop to make an online payment
He is wrong, but only because security software also makes a computer run faster
questions.explain: Attackers want the machine's connection, its processing power and the credentials typed on it, none of which depends on what is stored on the disk. A compromised laptop can be used to send spam, to join attacks on other targets or to capture his email and college logins, and it becomes a source of infection for the people he shares files with. The value of a computer to an attacker has very little to do with the files its owner keeps.
why_wrong: Malicious software does not inspect what a machine stores; a computer with no documents at all is still useful for sending spam, attacking others or mining.
Every login he types, from email to the college portal, can be captured whether or not he ever makes a payment.
Security software is not a performance tool, and the real reason he is wrong is the value of his machine and his accounts to an attacker.

questions.q: A full-screen page appears while Vidhi is browsing, complete with a scanning animation, an announcement that her computer is infected with thirteen viruses, a button offering a cleaner and a helpline number. Her own security software has said nothing at all. What is happening, and what should she do?
options: The page has found a real infection, so she should download the cleaner at once
She should ring the helpline, because a published number shows the warning comes from a real company
She should switch off her own security software, since it is clearly missing the infection
A web page cannot examine her computer, so this is a fake alarm and the offered cleaner would itself be malicious; she should close the page and scan with the software she installed herself
questions.explain: A page in a browser has no way of inspecting the files on your disk, so an animated scan and a precise count of infections are theatre designed to frighten you. The panic exists so that you install the offered program, which is the actual attack, or ring a fake support line that talks you into paying or into granting remote access. Closing the page or the browser and scanning with your own software is the whole of the correct response.
why_wrong: The download is the attack itself: a program offered by a page that has just frightened you is how malicious software gets installed voluntarily.
Anyone can print a telephone number on a web page, and fake support lines exist precisely to collect payments and remote access from frightened callers.
Turning off her own protection is exactly what the scam wants, since it removes the one thing that might block what she is about to install.

questions.q: Harsh installs a free video converter, clicking Next on every screen as fast as he can. Afterwards a new toolbar has appeared in his browser, his search engine has been changed and pop-ups show up on pages that never had them. What would have prevented this?
options: Installing the converter while logged in as administrator so that it installed correctly
Choosing the custom or advanced option during installation and unticking the extra software offered alongside the converter
Clicking Next even faster, since the extras are only added when an installer is left waiting
Restarting the computer straight after installing, which removes anything the installer added
questions.explain: Free installers are often funded by carrying extra advertising software, and the quick express path accepts those extras because they are pre-ticked on the screens most people skip. The custom or advanced route lists them so that each one can be refused, which is why it is worth the extra thirty seconds. Downloading from the maker's official site in the first place reduces the chance of extras being bundled at all.
why_wrong: Administrator rights would let the bundled extras install more deeply into the system, not fewer of them.
The extras were pre-ticked on the screens he clicked past; hurrying is what accepted them, not what avoided them.
A restart does not uninstall anything, and the toolbar and changed settings survive a reboot quite happily.

questions.q: An attachment in Simran's inbox is named Fee_Receipt.pdf.exe and her mail program shows a plain, unfamiliar icon for it. She was not expecting any receipt from anyone. What is the correct reading of this?
options: It is a program dressed up to look like a document, and running it would install whatever the sender chose, so she should not open it
It is an ordinary PDF that has been compressed for email, so opening it is safe
It is safe, because a document cannot carry anything harmful
It is safe to open as long as she deletes it immediately afterwards
questions.explain: The last extension is the one that decides how the system treats a file, and .exe means an executable program rather than a document. Writing .pdf in front of it is a disguise aimed at a reader who glances at the name and expects a receipt, and the unexpected arrival is a second warning sign. The safe response is to leave it unopened and delete or report the message.
why_wrong: Compression produces .zip or a similar archive; .exe is not a compressed document but a program.
Documents can carry harmful embedded content of their own, and in any case this file is a program rather than a document.
The damage happens the moment the program runs, and deleting the file afterwards cannot undo an installation.

questions.q: At the fee counter Aditya types his portal password on a shared terminal. A man waiting just behind him leans in slightly each time Aditya's fingers move and glances away whenever Aditya turns around. Nothing has been installed on the terminal and no message or call was involved. Which technique is the man most likely using?
options: Baiting
Keylogging
Shoulder surfing
Pretexting
questions.explain: Shoulder surfing is the simplest attack of all: the attacker just watches the victim enter a password, PIN or OTP from close by. It needs no software, no message and no conversation, only physical proximity, which is why shielding the keyboard and being aware of who is standing behind you matters at counters, ATMs and lab machines.
why_wrong: Baiting leaves something tempting, such as an abandoned USB drive or a free download, for the victim to pick up on their own; nothing is being offered here.
A keylogger is software that must first be installed on the machine to record keystrokes, and the scenario states that nothing was installed.
Pretexting needs an invented scenario and a false identity used in conversation, but this man never speaks to Aditya at all.

questions.q: A message posted in Sneha's class group offers a free lifetime licence for a paid coding platform, normally costing three thousand rupees, to anyone who sends their roll number and college portal password so that the sender can link the licence to their account. Which social engineering technique is this?
options: Quid pro quo
Dumpster diving
Tailgating
Shoulder surfing
questions.explain: Quid pro quo means something for something: the attacker dangles a service, gift or upgrade and asks for credentials or access as the price. It works because the victim feels they are receiving a bargain rather than being robbed. No genuine service ever needs your account password in order to give you something.
why_wrong: Dumpster diving means recovering useful information from discarded papers, printouts or old devices, which is not what is happening here.
Tailgating is following an authorised person through a door or barrier to get into a restricted physical space.
Shoulder surfing means watching someone type their credentials from nearby; here the victims are asked to hand them over willingly.

questions.q: A man in a service company uniform walks into the department office, says he has been sent for the quarterly UPS inspection, quotes a work order number and the name of the lab in charge, and asks the clerk to unlock the server room for him. No such visit had been scheduled. Which technique is he using?
options: Tailgating
Pretexting
Baiting
Dumpster diving
questions.explain: Pretexting is building a believable scenario around a false identity so that the target hands over information or access without questioning it. The uniform, the invented work order and the real name of a staff member all exist to make the story hold together. The defence is verification through a known channel: ring the lab in charge before opening anything.
why_wrong: Tailgating means slipping in behind someone who has opened a controlled door, without presenting any identity or story; this man walks up and asks openly.
Baiting relies on leaving something tempting for the victim to pick up or run, such as a labelled USB drive or a free download.
Dumpster diving is searching an organisation's discarded paper and hardware for useful details, not talking your way into a room.

questions.q: An email reaches only the eight students of one project group. It uses their guide's real name, the exact project title discussed at last week's review, and asks each of them to sign in at a link to upload the corrected report. No other student in the batch received anything like it. This attack is best described as:
options: Whaling
Smishing
Spear phishing
Quid pro quo
questions.explain: Spear phishing is aimed at a small, chosen set of targets and is made convincing with real details gathered about them, rather than being blasted out to thousands of addresses. The accuracy of the guide's name and the project title is the giveaway that the attacker did homework first, and it is exactly what makes such mail so much more effective than bulk phishing.
why_wrong: Whaling is targeted phishing aimed at a senior figure such as a director, principal or chief executive, whereas these recipients are ordinary students.
Smishing is phishing delivered by SMS, and this arrived as email.
Quid pro quo dangles a benefit in exchange for information, but nothing is being offered to these students.

questions.q: Rahul receives an email that looks exactly like his bank's, addresses him by his full name, and opens a page showing https and a closed padlock. He is still uneasy. Which check would give him the most reliable answer about whether the notice is genuine?
options: Confirm that the page shows https and a padlock, because a fraudulent site cannot obtain those
Treat the full name as proof, because a stranger would not know it
Reply to the email and ask the sender to confirm that the message is genuine
Ignore the link entirely, open the bank's site by typing the address himself or through the official app, and see whether the same notice appears there
questions.explain: The only trustworthy test is to reach the organisation through a channel you already know is genuine and check whether the claim exists there. Everything visible inside the suspicious message, including the design, the padlock and your own name, is under the attacker's control or easily obtained. Going to the real site yourself removes the attacker from the path altogether.
why_wrong: A padlock and https only mean the connection to that page is encrypted; anyone, including an attacker, can obtain a certificate for a lookalike domain.
Full names, phone numbers and even account details circulate in leaked data, so personalisation is cheap and proves nothing.
A reply goes straight back to the attacker, who will simply confirm that the message is real and now knows the address is read by a live person.

questions.q: A caller to the accounts office quotes last month's internal file reference numbers and the names of the two clerks who signed a particular form, and sounds entirely genuine because of it. An inspection afterwards finds that the office's old printouts and photocopy rejects go straight into an open bin behind the building and are never shredded. How did the attacker most likely gather those details?
options: Tailgating
Dumpster diving
Shoulder surfing
A brute force attack on the office email account
questions.explain: Dumpster diving is collecting information from what an organisation throws away: printouts, internal forms, notes and old storage devices. Details that look harmless on paper, such as reference numbers and staff names, are precisely what makes a later phone call sound authentic. Shredding paper and wiping or destroying old media closes this route.
why_wrong: Tailgating would put the attacker physically inside a restricted area, which the scenario gives no sign of and which is not needed to reach an open bin outside.
Shoulder surfing means watching someone type or read something on a screen from nearby, which would not yield month-old file references.
A brute force attack means guessing a password by trying huge numbers of combinations; nothing here suggests any account was broken into.

questions.q: Meera spots an obvious phishing email in her college inbox pretending to come from the exam cell. She has not clicked anything in it. What is the best thing for her to do?
options: Forward it to her class group so that everyone can see the exact message and stay alert
Click the unsubscribe link at the bottom so that the sender stops writing to her
Report it to the college IT helpdesk through its official contact, then delete it without clicking anything
Reply to the sender saying that she knows it is a scam
questions.explain: Reporting lets the people who run the mail system warn everyone and block the sender, which protects far more than one inbox. Anything that sends a signal back to the attacker, or that puts the live message in front of more people, makes the situation worse rather than better. Warning classmates is fine, but do it in your own words, without the working link attached.
why_wrong: Forwarding puts a live malicious link into many more hands, and someone in a hurry will click it.
Unsubscribe links in phishing mail are usually just another attacker-controlled link, and using one confirms that the mailbox is active.
A reply tells the attacker the address is read by a real person, which makes it a more valuable target for the next attempt.

questions.q: A message from an unknown number reaches Karan on a chat app. It carries his friend's name and profile photo, says his friend's phone was stolen and this is a temporary number, and asks Karan to send five thousand rupees urgently to a payment id. What should Karan do?
options: Call his friend on the number he has always used and treat the request as fake until his friend himself confirms it
Send a smaller amount first, since a genuine friend in trouble needs at least something
Ask the new number a personal question, since only the real friend could answer it
Check the profile photo closely, since a stranger could not have his friend's picture
questions.explain: When a request for money or credentials arrives unexpectedly, the fix is verification through a channel you already trust, not closer inspection of the suspicious message itself. Urgency and a familiar identity are the two levers social engineering pulls hardest, and both are designed to stop you from making that one check. If the friend really has lost his phone, a short delay costs nothing.
why_wrong: A smaller payment is still a payment to a stranger, and complying once marks Karan as a target for repeated requests.
Answers to personal questions are often visible on social media or in old group chats, so this test is easy to pass.
Profile photos are public or easily copied from social media, so an identical picture proves nothing about who is typing.

questions.q: A project team's web server inside the college network cannot be reached from the hostel block. A junior administrator suggests switching the firewall off completely until the demonstration is over. What is the right way to solve this?
options: Switch the firewall off for the demonstration and turn it back on the same evening
Add a rule allowing traffic to that one server on the single port the web service needs, and leave everything else blocked
Allow every incoming connection from the hostel block, since those machines belong to the college
Replace the firewall with an antivirus program on the server, since antivirus covers the same ground
questions.explain: A firewall is meant to permit exactly what is required and deny the rest, so the correct fix is the narrowest rule that makes the service work. Turning protection off, or opening a whole range of addresses, exposes every other service on the network for the sake of one demonstration. The same least privilege thinking that governs user accounts governs firewall rules.
why_wrong: An unprotected window is enough: automated scanning of exposed networks is continuous, and people routinely forget to switch protection back on.
Machines inside the college can themselves be infected or borrowed, so trusting a whole block wholesale gives away far more access than the demonstration needs.
Antivirus inspects files on a machine for malicious content; it does not decide which network connections are allowed in, so it cannot replace a firewall.

questions.q: A department audit discovers that three students who graduated last year still have working logins on the project server, and that one of those logins was used last month from an unfamiliar location. Which measure deals with the cause most directly?
options: Make every current user change their password every fifteen days
Install a hardware firewall at the department's router
Move all users from SMS one-time passwords to an authenticator app
Disable or remove an account as soon as its owner no longer needs it, and review the list of accounts regularly
questions.explain: Access should last only as long as the reason for it. An account nobody is watching but everybody has forgotten is an open door: no one notices unusual use, and its password is unlikely ever to change. Regular review and prompt removal of accounts is basic account management and the direct answer to accounts that outlive their owners' need.
why_wrong: Frequent password changes affect only accounts still in use; a forgotten account's owner is not there to change anything.
A firewall controls which network connections are allowed, but these logins are legitimate credentials arriving through the normal route.
A stronger second factor helps current users, yet the underlying problem is that these accounts should not exist at all.

questions.q: Ishita's phone loses mobile network in the middle of an ordinary day with no explanation. Within the hour her email and payment accounts have been reset and taken over. Her passwords were never shared, her laptop is clean, and both services sent their one-time codes by SMS. What most likely happened, and what would have reduced the risk?
options: Her number was taken over through a SIM swap, so every SMS code reached the attacker; codes from an authenticator app or a hardware key would not have followed the number
Old SMS codes were reused because they never expire, which a longer password would have prevented
A rootkit on her laptop was reading her screen, which the laptop's firewall should have blocked
Both passwords were guessed by brute force, which changing her passwords every week would have prevented
questions.explain: In a SIM swap the attacker persuades the mobile operator to move the victim's number onto a new SIM, which is why the real phone suddenly goes dead just before the accounts fall. Every SMS code then arrives at the attacker's handset. An authenticator app generates its codes on the device itself and a security key is a physical object, so neither travels with the phone number.
why_wrong: One-time codes are short lived and single use by design, and no password length affects a code sent to the wrong phone.
The scenario states the laptop is clean, and the sudden loss of mobile network points at the number, not the machine.
Brute force guessing does not explain why her phone lost signal at the same moment, and the resets were driven by codes rather than by passwords.

questions.q: Two of Vikram's accounts used different passwords. Cricket@2020 was broken within minutes, while otter-lantern-copper-drift survived the same attack. Neither password had appeared in any leak, neither was typed into a fake page, and both sites protect stored passwords in the same way. What explains the difference?
options: The second contains hyphens, and passwords containing punctuation cannot be cracked

The first is an ordinary word with a predictable pattern that sits in cracking wordlists, while the second is long and unpredictable enough that guessing it would take an impractical number of attempts
Length makes little difference; what mattered is that the first password was used on a website and the second was not
The second uses no digits or capital letters, so cracking programs ignore it
questions.explain: Cracking tools do not grind blindly through every combination first; they start with common words and the patterns people add to them, such as a capital at the front, a symbol and a year at the end. Cricket@2020 is that pattern exactly. A long string of unrelated words has no pattern to exploit, and each extra character multiplies the number of possibilities, which is why length is the single biggest contributor to strength.
why_wrong: Punctuation adds a little variety but nothing is uncrackable because of it; the first password contains a symbol too.
Both passwords were used on websites, so that cannot be the difference, and length is precisely what matters.
Cracking programs do not skip passwords for lacking digits or capitals; an all lowercase passphrase is strong because of its length and unpredictability.

questions.q: A college portal lets anyone reset a password by answering two questions: the user's date of birth and the name of their school. Birthdays are wished publicly in class groups every year and most students list their school on social media. What is the real problem here?
options: The problem is only the number of questions; asking three instead of two would make the reset safe
There is no problem, since the portal still demands a strong password at the normal login screen
There is no problem, because two separate questions already amount to multi-factor authentication
The reset path can be answered from publicly available information, so it becomes the weakest way into the account no matter how strong the password is
questions.explain: An account is only as strong as the easiest route into it, and password recovery is a route. If the recovery answers are facts anyone can look up, an attacker simply bypasses the password instead of attacking it. Good recovery uses something genuinely secret or a registered second factor, not biographical details that the user broadcasts every year.
why_wrong: More questions of the same kind still draw on public facts, so the attacker just looks up one more thing.
The strong login password is irrelevant when the reset path replaces it without ever asking for it.
Both questions test things the user knows, and neither is secret, so this is one weak factor rather than two.

questions.q: A visiting speaker asks to use a lab computer for twenty minutes to open his slides from his email. The machine has an administrator account used by the technician and separate standard accounts for the staff. Which arrangement follows the principle of least privilege?
options: Let him sign in with the technician's administrator account, so that nothing is blocked while he works
Lend him a staff member's own standard account and password for the twenty minutes
Let him use the restricted guest account, which cannot install software or reach other users' files
Create a new administrator account for him and delete it after the talk
questions.explain: Least privilege means giving exactly the access the task needs and nothing more. Opening a browser and a slide file needs no ability to install software, change settings or read anyone's files, which is precisely what a guest account is for. It also keeps the visitor's activity separate from any staff member's identity on that machine.
why_wrong: Administrator rights would let anything he runs, including anything hidden in a downloaded file, change the whole system.
Sharing a personal account gives him access to that person's files and makes everything done in the session appear under their name.
A brand new administrator account gives the same excessive rights, and an account created in a hurry is exactly the kind that is forgotten rather than deleted.

questions.q: Aarti keeps her laptop's own firewall switched off, arguing that the hostel router already has one. She also uses the laptop on cafe and airport Wi-Fi several times a month. Why is her reasoning unsafe?
options: Because a router's firewall inspects only outgoing traffic, while a laptop's firewall inspects only incoming traffic
Because the router's firewall protects only traffic passing through that router; away from it, and against other machines sharing the same public network, only the laptop's own firewall applies
Because a router's firewall stops working as soon as more than one device is connected to it
Because the laptop's firewall is the component that scans downloaded files for viruses
questions.explain: A hardware firewall built into a router guards the boundary of one network, so its protection ends the moment the laptop leaves that network. On a cafe or airport network the laptop sits alongside strangers' machines, and traffic between them never passes the hostel router at all. The software firewall on the machine travels with it, which is why both layers are kept on.
why_wrong: Both kinds of firewall can filter traffic in either direction; the difference between them is what they protect, not which direction they watch.
A router firewall is designed to serve every device on the network at once, and the number connected does not disable it.
Scanning files for malicious content is the job of antivirus software; a firewall decides which network connections are allowed.

questions.q: Rohit checks his results on a cyber cafe computer. The browser offers to remember his password and he is in a hurry to get to class. Which course of action is right?
options: Let the browser save the password, since he has chosen a long one that nobody could guess
Simply close the browser window, because closing it signs him out of the account
Leave the session signed in but lock the screen, so that the next user has to ask the cafe owner for help
Refuse to save the password, sign out of the account and close the session, or use a private window from the start
questions.explain: On a machine you do not control, the only safe assumption is that anything left behind will be found by the next user. Signing out ends the session on the server, which is what actually revokes access, and refusing to save the password keeps it out of the shared browser. A private window helps because it discards cookies and history when it closes, but signing out properly still matters.
why_wrong: A saved password can be read or simply used by the next person at that machine, however strong the password itself is.
Closing a window usually leaves the session cookie in place, so reopening the browser can walk straight back into the account.
A screen lock on a shared cafe machine protects nothing; the staff or the next user can unlock or restart it, and the session is still open.

questions.q: Before an internship interview Nandini searches her own name and finds three-year-old public posts, a photo of her uploaded and tagged by someone else, and an old comment left under her real name on a blog. She deletes her own posts. What should she understand about the rest?
options: Material posted by other people, or already copied, cached or archived, can stay visible after her own copies are gone, so she should also review her privacy settings and ask those people to take their posts down
Deleting her own posts removes everything, because every other copy points back to the original
Only well-known people have old content that lingers; an ordinary student's material disappears within a year
Searching her own name in a private window will stop those results from appearing in other people's searches
questions.explain: A digital footprint is not one file you can delete.
