It is spread across other people's accounts, search engine caches, archives and the screenshots of anyone who saw it, so removing your own copy shrinks the footprint without erasing it. The practical response is to tighten privacy settings, ask others to remove what they posted about you, and be deliberate about what goes online in the first place.
why_wrong: Copies on other accounts, in caches and in archives are independent of the original and survive its deletion.
Anything public can be indexed, saved or screenshotted regardless of how well known its author is.
A private window only affects what her own browser stores; it has no effect on what search engines show anyone else.

questions.q: Arjun's group needs a paid design tool for a two-week project. A classmate offers a cracked installer with the licence check removed, while the maker also offers a free trial and a free student licence. What is the right judgement?
options: It is acceptable, because the work is academic and nobody is earning money from it
It is acceptable, as long as they uninstall the tool once the project has been submitted
It is acceptable, provided they credit the software's maker in their report
They should use the trial or the free student licence, because the cracked copy is copyright infringement and a modified installer is also a common way of delivering malware
questions.explain: Software is licensed, not simply owned, and removing the licence check is a breach of that licence however the copy is used. There is also a practical risk: someone has already altered the program's code, and altered installers are one of the classic ways Trojans and ransomware reach a machine. Here the legitimate free routes cost nothing, so the unlicensed copy has no justification at all.
why_wrong: Non-commercial use does not turn an unlicensed copy into a licensed one; academic use is covered by the maker's own student licence, not by ignoring the licence.
Uninstalling afterwards does not undo the unlicensed use, and anything the modified installer left behind stays on the machine.
Crediting the maker addresses attribution, which is a different obligation from paying for or being licensed to use the software.

questions.q: While viewing his own marksheet, Deepak notices that changing the roll number in the page's web address displays another student's marksheet. He is curious about how far the fault goes. What is the ethical course of action?
options: Try a handful of other roll numbers first so that he can describe how serious the problem is, then report it
Stop at once, report the fault to the department or the portal's administrators with enough detail for them to reproduce it, and not open or pass on anyone else's data
Post the trick in the class group so that everyone can look up their friends' results
Say nothing, since he did not break in and the mistake is the college's
questions.explain: Finding a flaw by accident is not wrong; deliberately using it to read other people's data is, because consent and authorisation do not depend on how easy access turns out to be. The responsible path is to stop, report privately and precisely, and let the people who own the system fix it. Deepak has already seen enough to describe the fault without opening a single extra record.
why_wrong: Each extra record he opens is another person's private data viewed without authorisation, and one example is already enough for the administrators to reproduce the fault.
Publishing the method turns one accidental discovery into a mass privacy breach before anyone can fix it.
Staying silent leaves every student's results exposed, and knowing about a fault creates a responsibility to report it.

questions.q: A classmate sends Priya a screenshot of a private chat in which a third student describes a family problem. Priya finds it sad rather than amusing and thinks the class ought to rally round him. May she forward it to the class group?
options: Yes, because her intention is to help rather than to mock
Yes, provided she blurs out the name before forwarding it
No, because something shared in confidence should not be passed on without that person's consent, whatever the forwarder's intention
Yes, because the screenshot was sent to her and is therefore hers to share
questions.explain: Privacy belongs to the person the information is about, not to whoever happens to be holding a copy. Good intentions do not transfer that right, and the student concerned may have very sound reasons for telling one person rather than a group. The ethical course is to ask him what he wants, or to offer support directly, and to tell the classmate that the screenshot should not be circulating either.
why_wrong: Kind motives do not create consent, and exposing someone's private difficulty to a whole class can harm them however it is meant.
Blurring a name rarely anonymises anything, because the details of the story identify the person to anyone who knows him.
Possessing a copy of someone's words does not grant the right to publish them; the classmate should not have forwarded it in the first place.

questions.q: A free online quiz promising to reveal Kabir's ideal career asks, before showing the result, for his full name, date of birth, phone number, college email address and mother's maiden name. The site has nothing to do with his college. What is the sensible response?
options: Skip the quiz, because the result needs none of those details, and they are exactly the ones used to answer password reset questions and to make scam messages convincing
Fill it in, since the page shows https and a padlock, which means the data will be handled responsibly
Fill it in using his personal email instead of his college one, because then nothing important is exposed
Fill it in, since none of the details asked for is a password
questions.explain: A good habit online is to ask whether the information requested is actually needed for what is being offered, and a career quiz plainly does not need a date of birth or a mother's maiden name. Those particular items are classic answers to account recovery questions and the raw material for a convincing targeted scam. When a free service collects far more than its function requires, the data itself is usually the product.
why_wrong: A padlock only means the connection is encrypted in transit; it says nothing about who receives the data or what they do with it afterwards.
The email address is the least sensitive item on the list, and the date of birth and maiden name remain exposed either way.
Personal details of this kind are used to reset passwords and impersonate people, which can be as damaging as handing over a password.

questions.q: Yash's friend has a very slow connection and asks for Yash's college portal username and password so that he can download a question bank from the library section. He promises to sign out straight afterwards. What should Yash do?
options: Refuse, and offer to download the file himself and send it, because everything done under that login is recorded against him and remains his responsibility
Share the password and change it afterwards, which undoes any harm
Share it, since the library section holds nothing confidential
Share it on the condition that his friend opens no other part of the portal
questions.explain: An account identifies a person, so every action taken through it is attributed to the account holder, including anything the borrower does deliberately or by accident. The same login usually also reaches personal data such as marks, attendance and fee records, whatever the borrower intends to use. Sharing credentials is unnecessary here because Yash can simply fetch the file and send it.
why_wrong: Changing the password later does not undo anything done during the session, and the friend may have saved the credentials or stayed signed in on his own device.
One login normally opens the whole portal, including results and personal records, not just the section the friend wants.
A promise is not an access control; nothing in the portal enforces it, and a mistake or a shared device can expose far more.

questions.q: Kabir accidentally committed and pushed config.txt, which contains an API key. He then adds config.txt to .gitignore, commits that change and pushes again. Which statement is correct?
options: The key is now safe, because .gitignore removes the file from all earlier commits as well
The key is still exposed: .gitignore only stops untracked files from being added, and the earlier pushed commit still holds the key, so it must be treated as leaked and replaced
The key is safe, because .gitignore makes Git store the file in encrypted form
The key is safe as long as he never pushes again, since a push uploads only commit messages
questions.explain: A .gitignore entry decides which files Git starts tracking; it has no power over a file already being tracked and none at all over history that is already recorded. Every commit keeps the exact contents it captured, and anything pushed has already been copied to the remote for others to read. The only real repair for a leaked key is to revoke it and issue a new one, which is why secrets belong in .gitignore before the first commit.
why_wrong: Nothing in .gitignore edits past commits; the file stays exactly as it was recorded in the history.
Git never encrypts file contents; it stores them as they are, which is precisely why secrets must not be committed.
A push uploads whole commits, file contents included, and that upload has already happened.

questions.q: A file is staged with git add, then edited again in the editor, and only after that is git commit run. What does the resulting commit contain?
options: The latest version on disk, because Git always commits the current contents of a file
Nothing, because Git refuses to commit a file that changed after it was staged
The version of the file as it was when git add was run, while the later edit stays as an unstaged change
Both versions, stored one after the other inside the same commit
questions.explain: git add copies the file's contents as they are at that moment into the staging area, and git commit records exactly what the staging area holds. An edit made afterwards lives only in the working directory, so git status will still report that file as modified even after the commit succeeds. Running git add again before committing is what pulls the newer version in.
why_wrong: Git commits what was staged, not whatever happens to be on disk at the instant of the commit.
Git raises no objection at all; it commits the staged version and leaves the newer edit unstaged.
A commit is a single snapshot, so it cannot hold two different versions of the same file.

questions.q: Aditi runs git push and Git refuses it, reporting that the remote contains work she does not have locally. Her teammate pushed to the same branch an hour ago. What should she do?
options: Run git pull to bring the teammate's commits into her branch, settle any conflict, and then push again
Force the push, so that her version replaces whatever is on the remote
Clone the repository again into a new folder and copy her files across
Run git commit once more, since the rejection means her work was never committed
questions.explain: Git rejects a push that would leave the remote's commits behind, because accepting it would discard a teammate's work. The normal cure is to bring their commits into your branch first, using git pull or a fetch followed by a merge, resolve anything that clashes, and push the combined result. Her own commits sit safely in her local repository throughout.
why_wrong: Forcing the push overwrites the teammate's commits on the remote, which is exactly the loss the rejection was preventing.
A fresh clone merges nothing; she would still have to combine the two sets of commits, and copying files over abandons her history.
The rejection concerns the state of the remote; her work is already committed locally, and another commit adds nothing.

questions.q: Meera creates a branch called feature, commits a new file report.txt on it, then runs git checkout main. report.txt is no longer in the folder. What has happened?
options: The file was permanently deleted because she never pushed the branch
Her commit silently failed, which is why the file is not there
Git moved the file into .gitignore when she switched branches
Her folder now shows main's content; the commit and the file still exist on feature, and switching back or merging brings them into view
questions.explain: A branch is a separate line of commits, and checking one out makes your working folder match that branch exactly. report.txt was committed on feature, and main never received that commit, so main's snapshot has no such file. git checkout feature brings it back on screen, and merging feature into main adds it there for good.
why_wrong: Nothing is lost by switching branches; the commit is stored in the repository whether or not it was ever pushed.
A failed commit would have printed an error, and the file would still be sitting in the folder as an unstaged change.
.gitignore is a file you write yourself; Git never adds entries to it, and switching branches does not touch it.

questions.q: Aarav forked a public project two months ago. The original has had dozens of commits since, but his fork on GitHub still shows the old code. What is going on?
options: His fork is broken, because a fork is meant to mirror the original automatically
A fork is a copy taken at the moment he made it and does not update by itself, so he must bring the original's new commits into his fork
The original project must have undone its recent work, since a fork always matches its source
Forks update only for users who have starred the original repository
questions.explain: Forking copies a repository into your own account at that instant, and from then on the two are independent; your fork changes only when you change it. Before writing a fix it is worth pulling the newest commits from the original into your fork, so the work is built on current code. Otherwise a pull request can arrive cluttered with differences that have nothing to do with the fix.
why_wrong: Nothing has broken: forks are independent copies by design, not live mirrors.
The original's history is untouched; it is his own copy that stayed where it was.
Starring only bookmarks a project and changes nothing about any repository's contents.

questions.q: Ishan and Rhea both edited style.css on separate branches - he changed the first few rules, she changed the last few. The merge completed with no conflict at all. Why?
options: Because one of them committed first, and Git keeps the earlier commit's version of a file
Because Git quietly kept one version and discarded the other to avoid a conflict
Because Git merges changes region by region, and a conflict is raised only when both sides changed the same lines
Because work done on separate branches can never conflict
questions.explain: A merge compares what each side changed against their common starting point, region by region inside the file. Two sets of edits in different parts of the same file combine cleanly and both survive in the result. Git stops and asks you to decide only when the two sides rewrote the same lines, because that is the one case where it cannot tell which version was intended.
why_wrong: Git does not favour whoever committed first; both sets of changes are applied.
Git never discards a change silently; when it cannot combine two versions it halts and reports a conflict.
Conflicts are precisely what happens when branches touch the same lines, so separate branches are where most conflicts come from.

questions.q: Sneha creates a new file secrets.env inside her repository, but git status reports nothing to commit and never lists the file as untracked. The file is definitely in the folder and is not empty. What is the most likely reason?
options: A pattern in the repository's .gitignore matches the file, so Git deliberately leaves it out of the listing
Untracked files never appear in git status until they have been staged with git add
git status lists only files that were part of an earlier commit
Git skips any file whose name it does not recognise as a normal source file
questions.explain: git status normally lists a brand-new file under untracked, so a file that never appears at all is a strong sign it is being ignored. Entries in .gitignore tell Git to skip matching files completely, which is why that file is the standard place to list secrets and build output. What she is seeing is the protection working as intended, not a fault.
why_wrong: Listing untracked files is one of the main things git status does, long before anything is staged.
git status reports untracked and modified files as well as staged ones, so it is not limited to committed files.
File names carry no special meaning to Git beyond the patterns you yourself place in .gitignore.

questions.q: Varun clones the team repository, commits his work every evening, and pushes once a week. His laptop is stolen on a Thursday, four days after his last push. What is the position?
options: Nothing is lost, because Git is distributed and the remote automatically holds every commit he made
Everything is lost, including the work he pushed last Sunday
The commits he pushed on Sunday are safe on the remote; the four days of commits that existed only on the laptop are gone
Only his uncommitted edits are lost, since committing itself stores a copy on GitHub
questions.explain: Committing writes a snapshot into the repository on your own machine, and nothing reaches the remote until you push. Being distributed means every clone carries a full history, not that the copies keep themselves in step on their own. Pushing often is what turns the remote into a genuine backup of your work rather than just a sharing point.
why_wrong: A distributed system copies history only when somebody pushes, fetches or clones; it does not synchronise by itself.
Whatever he pushed on Sunday is on the remote, and any teammate can clone it back.
Commits are local; it is the push, not the commit, that places a copy on GitHub.

questions.q: Nisha opened a pull request from a branch in her fork. A reviewer asks for one more change, so she commits it on that same branch and pushes it to her fork. What happens to the pull request?
options: It stays frozen at the commits it held when it was opened, so she must open a new pull request
It is closed automatically, because the branch changed after review began
Nothing reaches it until she emails the new commit to the reviewer
It updates on its own to include the new commit, because a pull request follows the branch it was opened from
questions.explain: A pull request is a live proposal to merge a particular branch, not a fixed bundle of commits frozen at the moment it was opened. Every new commit pushed to that branch shows up in the same pull request, which is why review comments and fixes can go back and forth in one place. When the reviewer is satisfied, merging brings the whole branch in.
why_wrong: Pull requests are deliberately not frozen; answering review by pushing more commits is the normal flow.
Pushing to the branch updates the proposal rather than cancelling it.
Nothing needs emailing; the commits travel with the branch she pushed to her fork.

questions.q: Tanvi runs git fetch and sees that Git downloaded several new commits. She then runs git log on her branch and finds nothing new at the top. Is something wrong?
options: Yes - the fetch clearly failed, so she should clone the repository again
No - fetch put the commits into her repository but left her branch where it was, so she must merge them in, or use git pull, before they appear on her branch
Yes - git fetch downloads only commits she wrote herself, so her teammates' work never arrived
No - git log shows only commits made in the last 24 hours
questions.explain: Fetching and merging are separate steps on purpose: fetch brings the remote's commits safely into your repository, and merging is what moves your own branch onto them. Until she merges, git log on her branch quite correctly shows the same history as before. git pull is simply the two steps performed by one command.
why_wrong: Git reported the download, and a re-clone would throw away local work to fix a problem that does not exist.
Fetch brings down whatever the remote has that she lacks, which is mainly other people's commits.
git log shows the branch's whole history, however old the commits are.

questions.q: To free some space, Rudra deletes the hidden .git folder from his project. His project files are all still present, but git log now reports that this is not a repository. He had pushed to GitHub two days ago. What is true?
options: The folder is now an ordinary folder with no history, but the commits he had already pushed still exist on GitHub, so he can clone them again
Nothing is lost, because Git rebuilds .git automatically the next time a Git command is run
His project files were deleted along with the history, which is why Git cannot find anything
Running git init in the folder restores the old history
questions.explain: The .git directory is the repository: every commit, branch and setting lives inside it, while the files you see in the folder are just the currently checked-out copy. Deleting it leaves those files behind but throws the entire local history away. Only what he had pushed survives, because those commits were copied to the remote.
why_wrong: Git never restores a deleted history; a later command can only create a brand-new empty repository.
The working files sit outside .git, which is exactly why they are still in the folder.
git init starts an empty repository with no commits at all, so it cannot recover what was deleted.

questions.q: Anjali opens an email attachment named Invoice_March.pdf.exe, believing it is a bill. Nothing visible happens, but two hours later her documents are unreadable and a note on screen demands payment for the key. No other machine in the office is affected. How is this best described?
options: A worm that spread itself into her documents
A trojan horse, which is how it got in by deception, carrying ransomware, which is what it then did
A rootkit, because it waited two hours before acting
Adware, because a message appeared on her screen
questions.explain: The two names answer different questions. The disguise - a file dressed up as an invoice so the user runs it herself - makes the delivery a trojan horse, while encrypting the files and demanding payment makes the payload ransomware. Trojans very often carry some other kind of malware in with them, which is why both labels fit the same incident.
why_wrong: A worm spreads itself to other machines with no user action, yet here she had to open the file and no other machine was touched.
A rootkit works to hide itself and hold quiet administrator control; a delay is not what defines one, and a ransom note is the opposite of hiding.
Adware exists to push advertisements at the user; it does not encrypt files or demand a ransom.

questions.q: Which observation about a malware sample shows that it is a worm rather than a virus?
options: It appeared and ran on computers whose users never opened or ran any file
It deleted documents on every computer it reached
It arrived at the first computer as an email attachment
Some antivirus programs failed to detect it
questions.explain: A virus needs a host file and a human action to run; a worm is a standalone program that copies itself across a network on its own. So the deciding evidence is infection reaching machines where nobody opened anything, not how much harm was done or how the very first machine was reached. Damage and detection vary widely inside both categories.
why_wrong: Destructive behaviour is a payload, and viruses, worms and other malware can all carry destructive payloads.
Either kind can arrive first as an attachment; what separates them is whether spreading afterwards needs a user.
Escaping detection depends on how new or well disguised the sample is, and says nothing about how it spreads.

questions.q: Manish backs up his files every night to an external drive that stays plugged in permanently. Ransomware hits his PC, and he finds the copies on the external drive encrypted too. What does this teach?
options: That backups are useless against ransomware and paying is the only way out
That external drives are always encrypted by ransomware, while network folders are safe
That a backup protects you only if the malware cannot reach it, so at least one copy should be kept disconnected
That he should have backed up more often than once a night
questions.explain: Ransomware encrypts whatever the infected machine is able to write to, and a permanently attached drive is just another folder from its point of view. A backup helps only when it is out of reach at the moment of the attack, which is why one copy should be disconnected or otherwise protected from being overwritten. Checking that a backup actually restores matters just as much as making it.
why_wrong: Backups remain the most reliable defence; what failed here was leaving the copy connected, not the idea of backing up.
There is nothing special about external drives: any location the infected machine can write to, including a mapped network folder, is at risk.
More frequent copies onto the same connected drive would have been encrypted along with everything else.

questions.q: A server is suspected of carrying a rootkit. Antivirus scans run on the server itself report everything clean, yet several signs of intrusion remain. What is the sensible next step?
options: Accept the clean result, since antivirus running on the machine has the best view of it
Reboot the server a few times, because a rootkit cannot survive a restart
Give the antivirus administrator rights, which will let it see the hidden files
Examine the machine from outside the suspect system, for example by booting it from trusted clean media, and be prepared to reinstall the operating system
questions.explain: A rootkit's purpose is to sit deep in the operating system and misreport what is there, including to the security software running on that same system. Once a system cannot be trusted to describe itself, the answer is to inspect it from something known to be clean, and a full reinstall is often the only way to be certain. This is exactly why rootkits are counted among the hardest malware to deal with.
why_wrong: A tool that depends on the compromised system for its answers is the very tool a rootkit is built to deceive.
Rootkits are designed to load with the system and survive restarts, so rebooting changes nothing.
The problem is not missing privilege but a system that lies about its contents, and more rights do not restore trust.

questions.q: Ravi copies a game installer that turns out to be infected onto five lab computers, but he does not run it on any of them. The antivirus flags the file on all five machines, yet none of them behaves abnormally. Which explanation fits?
options: Copying rather than downloading the file is what made it harmless
It must be a worm, since the same malicious file reached five machines
A virus's code runs only when its host file is opened or executed, so the infection is present on all five but has not acted yet
The antivirus has already removed the danger simply by detecting and naming it
questions.explain: A virus is code riding inside a host file, and it does nothing at all until somebody runs that host. The five machines are carrying the infection without symptoms, and the first person to double-click it starts the damage. Needing a human action is exactly what separates a virus from a worm, which would have travelled between those machines by itself.
why_wrong: Copying a file does not alter its contents; the malicious code travels with it unchanged.
The file reached those machines because Ravi carried it there; a worm would have crossed the network without him.
Detecting and naming a file is not the same as quarantining or deleting it, and the file is still sitting there.

questions.q: Ira's antivirus is switched on and its definitions were updated this morning, yet a brand-new trojan she downloaded from an unofficial site still installed itself. Which explanation is correct?
options: Antivirus software checks only files that arrive by email, so downloads are never examined
Her antivirus must be a fake program, since genuine antivirus software catches everything
Detection leans heavily on recognising known patterns, so malware that is new or freshly repackaged can slip through, which is why careful habits still matter alongside the tool
Being up to date makes antivirus software check fewer files, which is how the trojan got through
questions.explain: Antivirus is one layer of defence, not a guarantee. Much of its work is comparing files against patterns of malware that is already known, so a sample nobody has catalogued yet can pass, especially when an attacker repackages it to look different. That is precisely why downloading only from official sources, and keeping backups, remain necessary even on a protected machine.
why_wrong: Antivirus software checks files from any source, downloads very much included.
Even genuine, well-regarded products miss new samples; no antivirus detects everything.
Updated definitions let it recognise more threats, not inspect fewer files.

questions.q: Devika suspects her laptop has adware. Which observation would point to adware most strongly, rather than to ordinary advertising on the web?
options: A news website shows advertisements between its articles
Pop-ups and advertisements appear inside pages that carry no advertising of their own, her home page has changed, searches are redirected, and it happens in more than one browser
A video site plays an advertisement before each video
A shopping site shows her products she looked at earlier
questions.explain: Advertising you meet on a website is placed there by that site, whereas adware sits on your own machine and changes what you see wherever you go. Advertisements appearing where a site has none, a changed home page, redirected searches, and the same behaviour across different browsers all point to software installed on the computer. Adware usually arrives bundled with a free download, so removing what was installed is where the fix begins.
why_wrong: Advertisements placed by a site are how many sites pay for themselves; that is normal web advertising, not adware.
An advertisement before a video is served by the video site itself and appears for every visitor.
Being shown products you viewed is ordinary tracking by advertising networks through cookies, not malware on the machine.

questions.q: On a shared lab PC, Sana works in an ordinary standard account. Ransomware runs in her session: her own documents are encrypted, but the system files and the other students' folders are untouched. What does this show?
options: That a standard account makes a machine immune to ransomware
That ransomware deliberately leaves system files alone
That malware acts with the privileges of the account that ran it, so it reached everything Sana could reach and nothing beyond that
That the ransomware failed and no data was actually lost
questions.explain: A program inherits the rights of the user who starts it, so working in a standard account puts a ceiling on how far malware can spread through the machine. That is a real reduction in damage, not immunity: everything the user can write to, their own documents included, is still fair game. The same reasoning is why administrator rights should be used only for the one task that needs them.
why_wrong: Her own documents were encrypted, so the account limited the damage rather than preventing the infection.
Ransomware encrypts whatever it can write to; here the account simply denied it access to the system area.
Her documents really were encrypted, which is a genuine loss unless a backup exists.

questions.q: Every night, all thirty machines in a lab send a huge volume of traffic to one particular external website. The number of affected machines has not changed in three weeks, and no new machines become infected. Which is the better explanation?
options: A worm, because many machines are infected and the network is busy
Adware, because the traffic is going to a website
A botnet, because a fixed set of infected machines is being directed at one outside target
Ransomware, because it happens at a scheduled time
questions.explain: Two details decide it: the infection has stopped spreading, and all the traffic points at one external victim. A worm would keep multiplying and the count of infected machines would climb; a botnet is a stable set of machines obeying a controller and attacking somebody else. Many machines flooding a single site at once is the pattern of a DDoS attack.
why_wrong: A worm's signature is continual self-spreading, and here the number of infected machines has been static for weeks.
Adware's effect is advertisements shown to the user, not thirty machines flooding one site at night.
Ransomware announces itself by encrypting files and demanding payment, and nothing is being demanded here.

questions.q: The IT team finds a trojan on one laptop, and alongside it a spyware program and a tool that connects the laptop to an attacker's server. The trojan never copied itself to any other machine. How should this be understood?
options: The trojan must really have been a virus, because more than one malicious program is present
The three programs must have come from three unrelated downloads, since a trojan cannot install anything
The trojan replicated itself into different forms, which is what trojans do on a single machine
A trojan does not copy itself to other machines, but once running it can open a backdoor and fetch further malware onto the machine it is already on
questions.explain: Saying a trojan does not replicate means it does not spread itself from computer to computer; it says nothing about what it may install where it already runs. A very common job for a trojan is to open a backdoor and pull down whatever the attacker wants next, which is how one deceptive download ends in several infections. Getting in by deception and then staying put is the defining pattern.
why_wrong: A virus is defined by infecting host files in order to reproduce, and nothing here reproduced.
Fetching additional malware is one of the commonest things a trojan does after installation.
Trojans do not replicate at all; what happened is that other programs were downloaded, not copies of the trojan.

questions.q: An email arrives from your project guide's genuine college address - the same address you have exchanged mail with all semester - saying she is stuck in a meeting and asking you to buy two online gift vouchers urgently and send her the codes. The domain is correct, the signature is normal, and there is no link or attachment. What is the right conclusion?
options: A matching sender address proves who wrote the message, so the request can be treated as genuine.
The message cannot be an attack because phishing always arrives with a link or an attachment to click.
The request should be confirmed by phoning her or meeting her, because a genuine address can belong to an account an attacker has taken over.
The message cannot be phishing because phishing always aims at passwords, never at money.
questions.explain: A sender address tells you which account sent the mail, not who was sitting at it. Once an attacker has the password to a real mailbox, every quick check you can make - domain, display name, signature - passes, which is exactly why an unusual request for money or secrets is confirmed through a separate channel that you choose yourself. Attacks that carry no link at all and work purely through a convincing instruction are common.
why_wrong: A sender address only identifies the account, and accounts get stolen; it is not proof of the person typing.
Many attacks carry no link or attachment and succeed purely on the instruction written in the text.
Phishing very often targets money, gift vouchers and bank transfers as well as credentials.

questions.q: A link opens a page that looks exactly like your bank's login page. The address bar shows a closed padlock, the certificate is valid, and the address reads https://secure.icicibank.verify-login.com. Which observation correctly identifies this page as a fake?
options: The real domain is verify-login.com, and icicibank is only a label the attacker placed in front of it.
The padlock proves the site is fraudulent, because genuine banks do not encrypt their login pages.
The word secure may be used only by authorised banking sites, so its presence gives the fraud away.
Nothing in the address can settle it; only spelling mistakes in the page text can reveal a fake.
questions.explain: In a web address the site you are actually on is named by the part just before the first single slash, read from the right: the owner here is verify-login.com, and everything to its left is a subdomain that owner may name anything, including a bank's name. A certificate and padlock only say the connection is encrypted and matches whatever domain you are on, and anyone can obtain one for a domain he owns. Reading the domain from the right is therefore the check that works.
why_wrong: Encryption is normal on genuine banking pages; a padlock says the connection is private, not that the site is honest or dishonest.
No such reservation exists; any site owner may put the word secure into a subdomain.
The address is decisive here, and careful fakes are often copied word for word with no spelling errors.

questions.q: On your college mail you receive an obvious phishing message claiming your account will be closed unless you confirm your password. You have clicked nothing. Your first instinct is to delete it and move on. What is the better response?
options: Reply to the sender saying you know it is a scam, so that your address is taken off their list.
Report it to the college IT helpdesk through its reporting option and then delete it, since classmates are probably receiving the same message.
Forward it to the whole class group so that everyone can see the wording for themselves.
Leave it untouched in the inbox, because deleting evidence of an attack is itself a security violation.
questions.explain: A phishing mail sent to one account in an organisation is nearly always part of a batch aimed at many, so the useful action is the one that protects other people: telling the team who can block the sender and warn everyone. Deleting it is fine for you, but deletion alone leaves the attack running against every classmate who has not spotted it. Replying to the attacker or forwarding the live message spreads the risk instead of reducing it.
why_wrong: Replying confirms that your address is live and read by a human, which makes you a better target, not a worse one.
Forwarding the original puts a working malicious link into many more inboxes, where someone will eventually click it.
No such rule exists; once the message has been reported through the proper channel, deleting your own copy is normal.

questions.q: Late at night your phone shows a login approval notification for your college account, which you did not request. Seconds later someone calls, says he is from the IT security team running a verification check, and asks you to tap Approve. What is the correct reading of the situation?
options: Approve it, because a notification can only be triggered by the account's real owner and is therefore a harmless system test.
Approve it and then change the password, so that the verification check is not left half finished.
Ignore the notification and the call, and assume nothing further needs to be done.
Deny the notification and change the password at once, because somebody already has the password and only the second factor is holding them back.
questions.explain: A login prompt you did not start means someone has already got past the first factor - your password - and is now waiting on the second. Tapping Approve hands over the account, and the phone call exists only to talk you into that tap. Denying stops this attempt, but the password is still in the attacker's hands, so it has to be changed before he simply tries again.
why_wrong: The prompt is raised by whoever is typing the password into the login page, and in this case that is not you.
Approving first gives the attacker a live session; changing the password afterwards does not cancel access already granted.
Ignoring it blocks this one attempt but leaves the stolen password working for the next one.

questions.q: Someone phones a college helpdesk claiming to be Aditi, says she is locked out just before a viva, and answers every identity question correctly - date of birth, home town, roll number, her pet's name. The helpdesk resets the password and the account is taken over. Aditi had told the caller none of this. What best explains the attack?
options: The helpdesk software must have been infected by a virus that revealed her answers.
The attacker must have guessed all four answers by chance, which cannot be prevented.
Details Aditi had posted publicly on social media supplied the answers, turning her digital footprint into the raw material for a convincing pretext.
It was a phishing email, because every identity theft begins with a phishing email.
questions.explain: Security questions ask for facts about a person, and facts about a person are exactly what public profiles, birthday wishes and photo captions give away for free. An attacker collects them, builds a believable story and lets a helpful human do the rest, which is why what you publish quietly widens the ground an impersonator can stand on. Nothing had to be hacked for this to work.
why_wrong: No malware is needed when the answers are already published where anyone may read them.
Getting four specific personal facts right by chance is not a realistic explanation; they were looked up.
No email was involved at all, and impersonation can be built from public information alone.

questions.q: A message on your college account looks internal, carries the department letterhead, and reads: our systems are being migrated tonight, confirm your username and password within 24 hours or your account will be deleted. A friend says the deadline proves it is genuine, since real notices are urgent too. What actually settles it?
options: The deadline settles it, because a genuine IT department never puts a time limit in a notice.
The request settles it: an IT department that runs the system never needs your password, whatever the deadline says.
The letterhead settles it, because official templates cannot be copied into an email.
Nothing in the message settles it; the only way to know is to enter the details and see whether the site accepts them.
questions.explain: Urgency is a pressure tactic, not evidence, because genuine notices do carry deadlines as well. The unmistakable sign is the demand for a password: administrators can reset any account without ever learning what you chose, so a message that asks you to supply your password is fraudulent by that fact alone. Judge the request being made, not the tone it is made in.
why_wrong: Real notices often do carry deadlines, so urgency by itself cannot separate genuine from fake.
Letterheads, logos and signatures are trivially copied, so they prove nothing about who sent a message.
Typing your password into the page to test it is precisely the action the attacker wants; the request for it has already settled the matter.

questions.q: Your phone rings and the caller ID shows the same number that is printed on the back of your bank card. The caller says a fraudulent transaction is being attempted and that he must verify your identity before he can stop it. What is the correct response?
options: Hang up and dial the number on the card yourself in a fresh call before discussing anything, because a displayed number can be forged.
Continue, because a call showing the bank's own number can only have come from the bank.
Continue, but share only the card number and expiry date, since those are printed on the card anyway.
Stay on the line and ask the caller to prove himself by reading out your account balance, then proceed.
questions.explain: The number shown for an incoming call is supplied by the calling side and can be set to almost anything, so it is not evidence of identity. The reliable move is to end the call and start a new one to a number you obtained independently, from the card, the passbook or the official app, because a fresh outgoing call cannot be redirected by the person who rang you. A genuine bank is content with that; a fraudster is not.
why_wrong: Caller ID can be spoofed, so a familiar number on the screen is not proof of who is calling.
The card number and expiry are exactly the details used to make fraudulent payments; being printed on the card does not make them public.
An attacker who already holds leaked statement data can recite a balance, and staying on the line keeps you inside his script.

questions.q: Four students choose passwords for accounts on the same website. Assuming the site itself is not breached, which password is hardest for an attacker to break?
options: P@ssw0rd123! - twelve characters mixing upper and lower case, digits and two symbols
Aditi@2006 - her own name and year of birth with a symbol in the middle
brass-lantern-oat-village - four unrelated ordinary words joined by hyphens
Xk7$q - five characters chosen completely at random
questions.explain: Cracking programs work from wordlists and from the predictable letter-for-symbol substitutions people make, so a familiar word wearing decoration is tried early no matter how complicated it looks. A string of several unrelated words is long, and length is what multiplies the number of possibilities an attacker must grind through, while remaining memorable. Randomness helps only when there is enough of it, and five characters is nowhere near enough.
why_wrong: It is a dictionary word with the usual substitutions, a pattern cracking tools expand automatically and try near the beginning.
A name and a year of birth are personal facts an attacker can look up, and this shape is among the first things guessed.
Five characters is far too short: the entire space can be searched quickly however random the characters are.

questions.q: A hostel block sits behind the campus firewall, which filters everything passing between the campus network and the internet. A student plugs in an infected laptop, and within a day several other laptops on the same hostel network are infected too, while the firewall logs show nothing unusual. Why did the firewall not help?
options: Firewalls inspect only email, so an infection spreading by any other route is invisible to them.
The infected traffic travelled between machines on the same side of the firewall, so it never crossed the point where the firewall inspects traffic.
The firewall must have been switched off, because a working firewall blocks all malware everywhere on the campus.
Firewalls act only on wireless traffic, so laptops connected by cable are never covered.
questions.explain: A network firewall is a gatekeeper on a boundary: it can examine only the packets that actually pass through it, normally traffic moving between the internal network and the outside world. Two machines on the same internal network talk to each other directly and never present that traffic at the gate. This is why each machine still needs its own software firewall and antivirus even when it sits behind a network firewall.
why_wrong: Firewalls filter network traffic in general rather than email in particular; the limitation here is where the firewall sits, not what it reads.
Nothing suggests it was off, and even a perfectly working boundary firewall cannot police traffic that never reaches it.
Firewalls do not distinguish wired from wireless in this way; both kinds of traffic cross the same boundary on the way out.

questions.q: Rahul does his everyday work in a standard, non-administrator account. He opens a malicious attachment; the program starts, encrypts the documents in his own home folder, and then fails when it tries to install a service that would run at every startup. What does this show?
options: A standard account makes malware harmless, since the program could not finish what it set out to do.
A standard account makes no difference to malware; the outcome would have been identical under an administrator account.
The antivirus rather than the account type must be what stopped the second stage.
Least privilege limits the damage to what that account could already reach, but it does not stop the malware running or destroying that user's own files.
questions.explain: A program inherits the rights of the account that launches it. A standard account can read and write its owner's files, so malware running there can certainly destroy them; what it cannot do is alter system areas, install services or touch other users' data. That is the real value of least privilege - it caps how far the damage spreads rather than granting immunity, which is why it works alongside backups and antivirus instead of replacing them.
why_wrong: His own documents were encrypted, which is serious; only the system-wide half of the attack failed.
The outcome would have been worse as administrator, because the startup service would then have installed successfully.
The second stage stopped with a permission refusal; an antivirus that was working would have blocked the program before any encryption happened.

questions.q: Meera installs a password manager, lets it generate a different long random password for each of her forty accounts, and then has to choose the master password. She decides to reuse her email password as the master so that she has only one thing to remember. What is wrong with that plan?
options: The master password guards every other password, so it must be the one password that is long, unique and used nowhere else.
Nothing is wrong, because the vault is encrypted and the choice of master password therefore does not matter.
Nothing is wrong, provided the email password contains at least one symbol.
The mistake is using a password manager at all, since keeping passwords in one place can never be acceptable.
questions.explain: A password manager concentrates risk deliberately: forty weak reused passwords become forty strong unique ones, and in exchange there is a single secret that must be protected properly. Reusing a password that already exists on another service undoes that trade, because a leak anywhere that password was used now opens the whole vault. The master password should be long, memorised, used nowhere else, and backed by a second factor on the vault itself.
why_wrong: The encryption is unlocked by the master password, so the strength and uniqueness of that password is exactly what the vault's safety rests on.
A symbol adds almost nothing here; the fatal property is that the password is already in use somewhere else.
Managers are the standard advice precisely because they make unique passwords practical; the flaw lies in her master password, not in the tool.

questions.q: When Kabir switched on two-factor authentication, the site displayed ten one-time backup codes. He took a screenshot and left it in his phone's gallery, on the same phone that holds the authenticator app. The phone is later lost. What is wrong with the way he stored the codes?
options: Backup codes expire after a week, so they would have been useless by then in any case.
Screenshots are unsafe only because the image quality makes the codes hard to read later.
The codes exist for the situation where the authenticator is unavailable, so keeping them on that same device removes the only route back into the account.
There is nothing wrong: losing the phone automatically switches two-factor authentication over to SMS.
questions.explain: Backup codes are the fallback for exactly the case where the second factor cannot be produced - a lost, broken or wiped phone. Storing them on that phone means the factor and its fallback disappear at the same moment, and a screenshot in the gallery can also be read by anyone who ends up with the device unlocked. They belong somewhere separate, such as a printed copy kept safely or a different device.
why_wrong: Backup codes are not time-limited in that way; each stays valid until it is used or the set is regenerated.
Legibility is not the issue; the issue is that the rescue copy is lost together with the device it was meant to rescue.
No such automatic switch exists; a recovery method has to be arranged in advance, which is what the codes were for.

questions.q: Two firewalls are configured differently. Firewall A allows all traffic except what appears on a list of blocked items. Firewall B blocks all traffic except what appears on a list of permitted items. Which comparison is correct?
options: A is safer, because listing the known bad traffic is a more complete description of the threats.
They are equally safe, since both are firewalls and both work from a list.
B is safer, but only for hardware firewalls; software firewalls must allow by default.
B is safer, because anything the administrator has not thought of is refused rather than let through.
questions.explain: The difference lies in what happens to traffic nobody anticipated. A rulebook that permits by default waves every new or unforeseen service straight through until somebody notices and writes a block rule, while one that denies by default fails closed: the unexpected is refused and has to be approved deliberately. Denying by default takes more maintenance, and that is the price paid for the safer failure mode.
why_wrong: A list of bad things is never complete, and new or unknown traffic keeps arriving for A to wave through.
The default action for unlisted traffic is exactly what separates them, and it points clearly one way.
Both styles exist in hardware and in software firewalls; the default-deny idea does not depend on the form the firewall takes.

questions.q: An old shopping site leaks its user database. Weeks later somebody in another country signs in to Sneha's email with the correct password on the first attempt. Nothing on her laptop was infected. Which control, had it been in place beforehand, would have stopped that sign-in?
options: A longer and more complex password on the email account.
Multi-factor authentication on the email account.
An up-to-date antivirus program on her laptop.
The software firewall built into her laptop.
questions.explain: The attacker never broke the password, he was handed it, so every measure aimed at making a password harder to guess misses the point here. What defeats a correct password in the wrong hands is a second factor the attacker does not hold, such as a code from an authenticator app or a security key. Her laptop took no part in the attack, so controls sitting on it could not have interfered with it.
why_wrong: Length protects against guessing and cracking, but a leaked password is already known however long it was.
Antivirus deals with malicious programs on a device, and no malware was involved in this sign-in.
Her laptop's firewall filters traffic to and from her own machine, while the attacker connected to the mail service from his.

questions.q: While Anjali is reading an article online, a box appears asking for administrator permission to let an unfamiliar program make changes to the computer. She started no installation. What should she do?
options: Approve it, because permission boxes are produced by the operating system and are therefore always safe to accept.
Approve it once so that she can see the program's name, and uninstall it afterwards if it turns out to be unwanted.
Refuse it, because a change she did not initiate should not be granted administrator rights, and then scan the machine.
Restart the computer at once, since the box will not appear again after a restart.
questions.explain: The prompt is the moment at which a program must ask before it can touch the parts of the system a standard user cannot reach, and it is raised on behalf of whichever program requested it - the box being genuine says nothing about that program being honest. The rule that makes the prompt useful is simple: grant elevated rights only for an action you yourself just started. Refusing costs nothing if the request was legitimate, since you can always start the task yourself afterwards.
why_wrong: The box is genuine, but it is only relaying a request; what matters is whether the program behind it is one you asked for.
Approving is the irreversible step - once it runs with administrator rights it can embed itself deeply enough that an ordinary uninstall will not remove it.
A restart neither removes the program that asked nor tells her whether the machine is now compromised.

questions.q: In a cafe, Arnav's phone lists two open networks: Cafe_Free_WiFi and Cafe_Free_WiFi_5G. Both connect without a password. He joins the second because its signal is stronger and starts checking his email. What is the sound judgement here?
options: The stronger signal must be the cafe's own router, so his choice was the right one.
Either is fine, because a network that has no password cannot be run by an attacker.
Either is fine, because the phone would refuse to connect to a network that was not genuine.
A network name can be copied by anyone nearby, so he should confirm the correct name with the staff and keep sensitive accounts off open Wi-Fi.
questions.explain: Nothing stops a laptop or a pocket router from broadcasting a network whose name imitates the real one, and a strong signal only means the impostor is sitting close by. Everything typed through such a network passes through the attacker's equipment first. Asking the staff which network is theirs, keeping banking and mail off open Wi-Fi, and preferring mobile data or a VPN are the practical answers.
why_wrong: Signal strength tells you only how near the transmitter is, and an impostor in the same room will usually be nearer than the cafe's router.
Open networks are the easiest kind to imitate, precisely because no password has to be matched.
A phone cannot tell a genuine network from a copy with a similar name; it simply joins whatever it is told to join.

questions.q: Excited about his first semester, Ishan posts a clear photograph of his college ID card on a public profile, showing his full name, roll number, course, date of birth and the card's QR code. Beyond the obvious loss of privacy, why is this a poor idea?
options: Those details are exactly what an impersonator needs to sound convincing to a helpdesk or a classmate, and the post can be copied and kept long after he deletes it.
It is a problem only if the photograph is sharp enough to read, so a slightly blurred picture would be entirely safe.
It is not really a problem, because a roll number and a date of birth are not passwords.
The only risk is that the college may object to its logo appearing online.
questions.explain: Identity checks at helpdesks, hostels and offices lean on ordinary facts - name, roll number, date of birth - so publishing them hands an attacker a ready-made script for pretending to be you. A post also leaves your control the moment it goes up: it can be saved, screenshotted or indexed, and deleting the original does not recall the copies. The safe habit is to keep identifiers out of public posts in the first place.
why_wrong: Blurring one part leaves the rest, and anything readable at all is enough; the judgement is about publishing identifiers, not about image quality.
They are not passwords, but they are the answers to the identity questions that stand guard in front of passwords.
A complaint about a logo is trivial beside the risk of impersonation built from the personal details on the card.

questions.q: By changing a number in the address of the college result portal, Devika finds that she can open another student's marksheet. Nobody else appears to know. What is the right thing to do?
options: Post the trick on the class group so that students can protect themselves by checking their own pages.
Try it on a friend's roll number first, with his spoken permission, to be sure the flaw is real before saying anything.
Report it privately to the college IT staff, describing what she found, and not use it again.
Say nothing and simply avoid the page, since reporting it might make her look responsible for it.
questions.explain: Finding a weakness by accident is not wrongdoing; what she does next decides the ethics. A private report to the people who can repair it protects every student whose records are exposed, whereas further poking about - even from curiosity, even with a friend's blessing - means deliberately opening records she is not authorised to see. Publishing the method before it is fixed simply invites everyone else to exploit it.
why_wrong: Announcing an unfixed flaw publicly puts every student's marksheet within reach of anyone who reads the message.
A friend cannot authorise access to college records; the college controls that data, so repeating the trick is still deliberate unauthorised access.
Silence leaves everyone exposed, and a prompt honest report is exactly what distinguishes her from somebody who exploited the flaw.

questions.q: Needing an expensive design program for a project, Pranav downloads a cracked copy from a file-sharing site and argues that using it for college work makes it acceptable. What is the accurate response?
options: He is right: copyright rules do not apply when the purpose is education rather than profit.
It is copyright infringement whatever the purpose, and it also means giving an installer from an untrusted source administrator rights; free or student-licensed alternatives are the proper route.
It is acceptable so long as he deletes the program once the project has been submitted.
It is acceptable only if he pays for the software afterwards, which turns the copy into a trial.
questions.explain: Using software outside its licence is infringement regardless of motive, and study is not an exception to copyright - what does exist is a legitimate route, since many vendors offer free student licences and capable open-source alternatives exist for most tasks. There is a security cost as well: a cracked installer is an unknown program that you deliberately grant administrator rights to, which is one of the most reliable ways to pick up malware.
why_wrong: Education is not a blanket exception to copyright, and vendors that want to help students issue licensed student versions instead.
Deleting it later does not undo the unlicensed use, and anything the installer dropped on the system stays behind.
Paying afterwards does not retrospectively license the copy, and a cracked build is not a trial of anything.

questions.q: Sana backs up her project every night to an external drive that stays plugged into her laptop so that the backup can run automatically. Ransomware reaches the laptop, and she finds her documents and her backup both encrypted. What should she change?
options: Nothing about the backup; she should rely on the antivirus instead, since that is what failed.
She should back up more often, because a more recent copy would have survived.
She should keep the same drive attached but store the files in a folder with a less obvious name.
She should keep at least one copy offline or in a separate location, disconnected except while the backup is actually running.
questions.explain: Ransomware encrypts whatever the infected computer can write to, and a permanently attached drive is just another folder from the machine's point of view. A backup counts as a backup only when the failure that destroys the original cannot reach it, which means one copy kept disconnected or off the machine entirely - an unplugged drive, or cloud storage that keeps previous versions. Frequency and folder names change nothing about what the malware can reach.
why_wrong: Antivirus can fail, and that is precisely the case a backup exists to cover; leaving the backup exposed removes the last line of defence.
A more recent copy would have been sitting on the same attached drive and would have been encrypted with everything else.
Malware walks through the drive rather than reading folder names for hints, so renaming hides nothing from it.

questions.q: Down with fever, Vikram asks his roommate to sign in to the college portal as him and upload an assignment before the deadline, and gives him his username and password. Both think this is harmless, since the work really is Vikram's. How should this be judged?
options: It is still wrong: the account is personal and its owner answers for everything done through it, so he should upload it himself or ask the teacher for an extension.
It is fine, because consent from the account owner makes any use of the account legitimate.
It is fine, because no data was stolen and the file uploaded was genuinely his own work.
It is wrong only if the roommate opens other pages in the portal while he is signed in.
questions.explain: Login credentials stand for a person, so every action recorded under them is attributed to that person, and sharing them breaks the link between the record and what really happened. Once someone else is signed in, the owner cannot limit what is done and still carries the consequences of all of it. A genuine emergency is handled by talking to the teacher, not by lending an identity.
why_wrong: Consent does not settle it: the college, not the student, sets the terms of the account, and those terms make it personal and non-transferable.
The breach is the sharing of the credential and the false record of who acted, not the contents of the file.
The sharing is already the breach; whatever the roommate browses afterwards would only add to it.

questions.q: Kavya has postponed the update reminders on her laptop for four months because restarting is inconvenient. Her antivirus is current and her firewall is on. Why is postponing still a real risk?
options: It is not a risk: updates only add new features and change how things look.
It is a risk only for the operating system; updates to a browser or a PDF reader do not matter.
Updates close flaws that are already publicly known, and attackers deliberately hunt for machines on which those known flaws have not been patched.
It is a risk only because an unpatched machine runs more slowly, which makes attacks easier.
questions.explain: A security update is published because a weakness has been found, and publishing the fix also announces to the world where that weakness was. Unpatched machines become the easy targets, since an attacker has nothing left to discover and working attack code often circulates within days. Antivirus and a firewall help, but neither repairs the flawed code itself; only the update does that.
why_wrong: New features come with some updates, but many exist solely to repair security flaws that are already being exploited.
Browsers, document readers and plug-ins handle untrusted files from the internet and are among the most heavily attacked programs of all.
Speed has nothing to do with it; the risk comes from the unrepaired flaw, not from how fast the machine runs.
